title: Arizona Cardinals 2026 watch guide: Schedule, streamers for Jeremiyah Love's rookie year Here's how to watch Love and the Cardinals from September to January. Takashi Williams

For the first time in a while now, there is new shine around the Valley of the Sun. The Arizona Cardinals approach 2026 with refreshed efforts to build out a culture —  they’ve moved on from Jonathan Gannon after three lost seasons, and from Kyler Murray after seven years of trial and error.
New head coach Mike LaFleur arrives from the Los Angeles Rams, where he coordinate
full_text:
No. 3 overall draft pick Jeremiyah Love is set to dash through the desert. Diannie Chavez / The Republic via Reuters Connect
For the first time in a while now, there is new shine around the Valley of the Sun. The Arizona Cardinals approach 2026 with refreshed efforts to build out a culture —  they’ve moved on from Jonathan Gannon after three lost seasons, and from Kyler Murray after seven years of trial and error.
New head coach Mike LaFleur arrives from the Los Angeles Rams, where he coordinated the league’s No. 1 scoring offense. There’s talent around the lineup with first-team All-Pro tight end Trey McBride and newly extended wide receiver Michael Wilson. Marvin Harrison Jr. looks to make good on his huge upside with a head coach who has a long history of working with receivers.
Veteran Jacoby Brissett starts as QB1 over Gardner Minshew II and Carson Beck, a third-round selection in April’s draft. Jeremiyah Love, the No. 3 draft pick, should bolster a running game that ranked 31st last year so long as he stays healthy. The Notre Dame product is the preseason favorite for Offensive Rookie of the Year, despite missing time in August with an ankle injury.
Arizona gets to explore its options and find a future in real time. Let’s see if the Cardinals are up to the challenge of a tough schedule, with just three home games in their first nine contests. Make sure you’re following the Cardinals on The Athletic . “ Scoop City ,” our NFL newsletter, delivers updates from around the NFL, and “ The Athletic Football Show ” is a thorough podcast that provides a fun rundown on all the happenings in the league.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars former Cardinals pass rusher JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC, and it’s where you can find 10 Cardinals games through Week 17.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed…

full_text:
Bijan Robinson is elusive and tough to tackle on the field. But off it, coaches and teammates struggle to find something negative to say about him. Mark J. Rebilas / Imagn Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Miami Dolphins punter Bradley Pinion is a two-time Walter Payton Man of the Year nominee. He and his wife Kaeleigh made a mission trip to Africa with Compassion International and helped fund two child development centers in Tanzania. And he says Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson “might be the best human I’ve ever met in my life.”
Falcons offensive lineman Chris Lindstrom says when aliens land on Earth, Robinson should be one of the human race’s representatives at the summit. When Robinson signed the deal that briefly made him the highest-paid running back in NFL history (Jahmyr Gibbs would pass him three days later), offensive lineman Jake Matthews struggled to come up with something adequate to say about his teammate.
“It’s almost too hard to continue to express a way to sing his praises,” Matthews said. “Like, I don’t think the guy’s ever done anything wrong before. He’s just an all-around good human being.”
Lindstrom: “If there were 100 humans to represent humanity, we’re going to recommend that guy be on that short list. From the locker room, we are sending him out. The athletic ability, the talent, the quality of human he is. He is the best person, the most genuine, loving, caring person you can find.”
So, the NFL’s leader in yards from scrimmage the last three seasons (5,648 yards) is a great guy, too?
“I was cautioned by people, ‘You’re not going to think this guy is real when you talk to him,’” first-year Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said.
Frankly, it can all seem too good to be true. Matt Ryan admits he used to wonder exactly that. Atlanta’s president of football and all-time leading passer was traded away from the Falcons a season before the team drafted Robinson eighth in 2023. Like everyone else, he saw Robinson’s television appearances and social media clips and wondered if it could all be real. So Ryan called his former offensive coordinator and Robinson’s coach at Texas, Steve Sarkisian.
“Sark was like, ‘Dude, that’s every day,’” Ryan said. “I’ve gotten to know him over the last couple of years, and I think he’s a special person.”
Surely, somewhere in Robinson’s life, there’s dirt, right? If there is, Phil Gruensfelder hasn’t found it. Gruensfelder has been the athletic director at Robinson’s high school alma mater, Salpointe Catholic, in Tucson, Ariz., for 25 years. After Robinson ended a heated recruiting battle by picking the Longhorns in 2020, Gruensfelder’s phone rang.
“My wife’s first cousin’s son, Matt Rutherford, is the equipment manager for the University of Texas,” Gruensfelder said. “Matt’s mom reached out to me and said, ‘Tell me about Bijan.’ I said, ‘He’s the nicest kid you can be around.’ Through his three years at Texas, I would hear from Matt’s mom, and she’d say, ‘Matt can’t speak more highly about Bijan. He’s one of those kids that will stick around the locker room and make sure it’s cleaned up, make sure he meets every person who wants an autograph.’”
Gruensfelder once started a conversation in his local grocery store with a man wearing a Falcons’ No. 7 jersey.
“The guy said, ‘He is really that normal?’” Gruensfelder said.
The perpetually smiling 24-year-old plays the “College Football ’27” video game daily, like many men his age. Granted, he’s playing online with his best friend, the actor Jonathan Daviss, who stars in the Netflix series “Outer Banks” and is scheduled to play Snoop Dogg in an upcoming biopic. Robinson also has a relationship with Brazilian soccer star Vinicius Junior because they are clients of celebrity jeweler Leo Frost, and he’s buddies with French soccer superstar Kylian Mbappe. Robinson also texts regularly with Matthew McConaughey. There are more stars in his cell phone, but Robinson’s too chagrined to name them.
“I’ve met some cool people,” he said, “but I’ll keep that one in.”
When Robinson came to Atlanta, linebacker Kaden Elliss, a seven-year (and counting) NFL veteran, expected some entitlement. Then Elliss watched the running back sit through every special teams meeting during his rookie year.
“We’re looking, like, ‘Dude, we all know you’re never going to play special teams,’ but he sat there all year,” Elliss said. “He’s just got this humility to him.”
Elliss, now with the New Orleans Saints, spent three seasons in Atlanta with a locker next to Robinson’s, trying to see if there were any cracks in the running back’s foundation. When pressed to name even one, he could not.
“The premier athletes at the premier positions so often are what you’d call a diva — they’re often so selfish. Not Bijan,” Elliss said. “He’s got this smile, brings this joy every single day, whether he is sitting in his locker or playing on the field. It’s special, and it’s contagious.”
Elliss’ sentiment was echoed by more than a dozen current and former teammates, coaches and acquaintances in Robinson’s orbit, as a months-long attempt to find anyone with a discouraging word about the Falcons’ most marketable star came up empty. Informed by a reporter of the effort, Robinson responded the way he always responds, with the wide smile that made him a Colgate pitchman .
“You won’t find nobody,” he said confidently. “I’m telling you, man, this is just me. This is who God made me to be. I wake up, I smile, I say prayers, talk to God, I take my vitamins, and I go about my day. That’s just who I am — seriously.”
Seriously, Donald Nguyen, the director of sports medicine at Texas, said.
“I have zero dirt,” Nguyen said. “It’s true. He’s a saint.”
After Robinson signed his first NIL deal with Raising Cane’s, he regularly brought lunch for the Texas training staff, and he sang “Happy Birthday” to Nguyen’s daughter on FaceTime, the trainer said. It was a noticeable change for a staff member whose job can feel anonymous and taken for granted in a locker room.
“He always said hello. He treated everyone with respect,” Nguyen said. “He would get to know our families. The guy is amazing.”
Let Bijan be Bijan pic.twitter.com/78LKHJr7em
— Atlanta Falcons (@AtlantaFalcons) September 2, 2026
John Bianco, the Longhorns’ longtime director of communications, tried hard to think of anything that might help this quest. He could only come up with two things: Robinson’s Texas teammates said he was a “terrible” basketball player, and he stopped to talk to too many people coming off the field after games.
“I’d have to be like, ‘Coach will never get to his postgame speech if you take a picture with everyone walking off the field,'” Bianco said.
When Jacksonville Jaguars defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro arrived in Atlanta as a second-round draft pick in 2024, he was nervous about approaching the Falcons’ young star. He shouldn’t have been.
“The way he would talk to me was like he already knew me, just encouraging 24/7,” Orhorhoro said. “I have never heard him say a negative thing. He’s the same person on and off the field every single day. God-fearing baller. That’s all he is.”
“That’s the preacher’s son. He ain’t doing nothing wrong,” Falcons wide receiver Drake London said. “And even if he was, I wouldn’t snitch on my boy.”
“I don’t think it’s too good to be true. I think it’s just who Bijan is,” guard Matthew Bergeron said.
“Always in a good mood, always a happy guy, man of faith. I’ve got no dirt,” Pinion said. “And he’s an incredible football player. I don’t think he knows how good he is at football. But, yeah, I got nothing. His only fault might be that he’s too nice. He’s an amazing human being.”
“He had a book fair, and I don’t think people even have those these days,” Falcons safety Jessie Bates said.
Tight end Kyle Pitts and quarterback Michael Penix Jr. were the only Falcons brave enough to stand up to this deluge of goodwill and offer up anything resembling a complaint.
“His musical taste is subpar, in my opinion,” Pitts said.…

full_text:
New Highmark Stadium’s original Kentucky bluegrass looked pristine from the stands, but its roots never took hold. The Bills replaced it after two preseason games and two open practices. Joe Buscaglia / The Athletic
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. — George Toma is known as The Sodfather. He’s the most revered groundskeeper in sports history, overseeing every Super Bowl field until three and a half years ago.
What’s been happening at Highmark Stadium troubles him.
“That hurts me,” Toma said. “That’s terrible to happen at all, but so soon? Somebody fell asleep.”
After just two preseason games, the Buffalo Bills tore out the grass field they had installed in October 2025. The field went unused for 10 months, but its roots didn’t take hold. Large chunks of sod were repeatedly gouged out by the players in exhibition games against the Carolina Panthers and Pittsburgh Steelers, as well as two open practices showcasing the new $2.2 billion stadium.
After the preseason opener, one Bills player told The Athletic, “ The field is ass right now .” President of business operations Pete Guelli said the field was performing to expectations. This week, however, the team tore out all the grass and started over .
The Bills’ home opener against the Detroit Lions on “Thursday Night Football” is two weeks away — the first of three straight Highmark Stadium games in 18 days.
While resodding an entire NFL field is relatively common, experts find the circumstances surrounding Buffalo’s sudden tear-out disconcerting.
“I saw their press release and heard some of their rationale, and they probably ought to start their stories ‘Once upon a time,’” said an award-winning sports agronomist who has helped install dozens of NFL and college football fields over the decades. He requested anonymity to protect professional relationships.
“That’s the worst sod I’ve seen in the NFL in my career. I can’t even imagine how that could have happened.”
Buffalo switched to grass this year for the first time since 1972, when it left War Memorial Stadium, a bleak venue known as The Rockpile. The NFL Players Association has pushed owners to switch to grass stadiums. The union says 92 percent of its players prefer grass.
The campaign gained further traction this summer. The FIFA World Cup demands grass for its matches. When the tournament held games in 11 NFL stadiums, seven were forced to replace artificial turf with grass. Those venues have since returned to artificial turf for the NFL season.
“Yes, natural turf is safer in a perfect setting,” said Tony Dick, a sports management professor at Baldwin Wallace University and former Cleveland Browns assistant head groundskeeper. “But if you have the situation like you have in Buffalo — and I went back and watched the film — you cannot tell me that field was safer than the artificial turf they just left.
“I’m never putting Josh Allen on a field in that condition.”
NFL clubs replace their grass based on several variables, the biggest being climate and the number of events.
The Miami Dolphins resod eight to 10 times a year in the tropics, but Hard Rock Stadium simultaneously hosts University of Miami football and bowl games as well as soccer matches and major concerts year-round. The Denver Broncos resod twice a year — once in August after the summer concert season, and again in late autumn before the mile-high ground freezes.
The Steelers traditionally resod Acrisure Stadium’s entire field before the season, replace the grass between the numbers in October, and perform another full resod later that month. The University of Pittsburgh and local high school football also use their field.
But the Bills installed their Kentucky bluegrass in October 2025 and didn’t stage any events until a public practice on Aug. 8, one week before the Panthers preseason opener.
“We have consulted with the NFL and an independent expert who works with multiple NFL teams,” the Bills said in a statement to The Athletic. “These consultants recommended utilizing this three-week window before the home opener to install the sod. The NFL inspects every field and determines whether it meets league standards. We are confident that they are the appropriate group to ensure the field performs at the necessary level.”
An NFL spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
The agronomist acknowledged that he would know more about the field’s issues if he had the chance to examine it himself, but several mistakes seemed obvious to him.
“You could see brown spots throughout,” the agronomist said. “That looked like disease, probably dollar spot fungus or brown patch fungus because bluegrass is susceptible to that.”
He saw signs of overwatering and said the Bills may have misread the new field’s high percolation rate, a measurement of how fast water drains. He also suspected the grounds crew had not used enough wetting agents to slow the percolation rate and keep nutrients in the soil longer.
“I would have been overseeding the heck out of it, trying to draw that sod down a little bit,” the agronomist said. “I also would have pounded the top of the field with sand (for the Panthers-Bills game). When players were getting tackled, you should’ve seen plumes of sand coming off the grass. That at least would have held the field down, closed up the seams.”
Matteo Bartolotta has worked with the Bills’ director of grounds, Aaron Ramella, as recently as this summer, helping the Bills prepare St. John Fisher University’s grass fields for training camp. Bartolotta owns and operates M&K Turf in Auburn, N.Y.
“It’s a lot more common to replace sod fields than people think,” said Bartolotta, a Bills diehard and former season-ticket holder. “We do have the three-game stretch coming. If they wait, with that NFL test of playability, they might not have passed it if the conditions got worse. It’s not cheap, but I think it was the right choice.”
Similar to a doctor who would be hesitant to diagnose a patient he hasn’t examined, Bartolotta didn’t want to say for sure what was ailing Highmark Stadium’s ill field without having put his hands in the dirt.
Bartolotta did find it germane, however, to share the time he was hired by Merion Golf Club, the prestigious course outside Philadelphia that has hosted five U.S. Opens. He was summoned to solve an ongoing mystery on the greens.
“They were peeling like carpet,” Bartolotta said.
The final green was the putting area next to the clubhouse. It looked marvelous. Bartolotta asked the course superintendent and an assistant what the difference was.
“They just kind of looked at each other and chuckled,” Bartolotta recalled. “He said, ‘This one doesn’t have the precision air system underneath that the other ones have installed.’ So you’re telling me the greens that have the ability to heat and cool and suck out excessive moisture, those greens have weaker root structure than the one that’s just growing naturally with native soil?”
Even with all that money and innovation and pampering, the greens at Merion Golf Club weren’t stimulated to thrive. They merely existed.
“When you have the ability to give the root anything that it wants, the root doesn’t stress,” Bartolotta said. “It just lays back like it’s on vacation. You have to make grass work. When you give it everything — all the nutrients, all the fertilizer, all the grow lights — it doesn’t have to go and search. It just hangs out.”
Beneath Highmark Stadium’s grass are ventilation, heating, irrigation and vacuum systems. Myriad sensors track oxygen levels, temperature and moisture to the decimal point. The Bills invested in the latest grow-light technology to roll onto the field wherever too much shade encroaches.
“They have a control room that looks like the space shuttle control deck,” the agronomist said. “They’re practically God in how easily they should be able to grow grass. To lose that field is unbelievable.”
You probably wouldn’t be surprised to learn Toma, 97, prefers the old-fashioned methods. His famous “and then…

full_text:
Former Bears wide receiver DJ Moore has a new vision: helping the Bills and quarterback Josh Allen reach the mountaintop. Ken Blaze / Imagn Images
At Halas Hall, “last season” has become a bit of a four-letter word. Not because the Chicago Bears didn’t enjoy what they accomplished during a division championship season that also produced the franchise’s first playoff victory in 15 years. Rather, coach Ben Johnson sees very little value in looking backward when there is so much more to focus on ahead.
Thus, the Bears are crossing the bridge now from the preseason into the 2026 regular season with purpose plus an understanding of the heavy lift they face to achieve their next goals.
For what it’s worth, the team’s current 53-man roster includes 20 players who were not a part of last season’s emergence. Which means a handful of key contributors from 2025 have begun new chapters elsewhere, too. In defiance of the Halas Hall ordinance, and in preparation for Week 1, we’re removing the blinders and using peripheral vision to check in on a half-dozen former Bears who were instrumental in last season’s success but are now carving out new roles with new teams.
Last season: Moore’s 2025 season was difficult to interpret. His chemistry with quarterback Caleb Williams was inconsistent. And his season totals (50 catches, 682 yards) were career lows. Yet with a pair of stadium-shaking game-winning touchdown catches in unforgettable comeback wins over the rival Green Bay Packers — the second in the wild-card round of the playoffs — Moore cemented his place in Bears history.
Why he departed: With the Bears well stocked with talented young pass catchers — Colston Loveland, Rome Odunze, Luther Burden — general manager Ryan Poles chose to dangle Moore as a trade chip over the winter and found interested suitors in Buffalo GM Brandon Beane and new head coach Joe Brady. Brady overlapped with Moore early in the receiver’s career with the Carolina Panthers. An early March trade — with Moore and a Round 5 pick sent to Buffalo — brought the Bears back a second-round pick.
Contract situation: Moore is still playing on the four-year, $110 million extension the Bears gave him in the summer of 2024. He carries a base salary of $23.5 million for every season through 2029. Were the Bills to part with him before that, the dead cap money would be greatly reduced in 2028 ($13.3 million) and 2029 ($8.9 million).
The word from Buffalo: “If there’s one thing that has become abundantly clear, the Bills are all in on making Moore a humongous piece of their offense as their No. 1 receiver. This was Beane’s biggest swing at improving wide receiver since trading for Stefon Diggs in 2020, and Josh Allen has been hard at work to build the on-field connection since Moore’s arrival.
“As camp moved along, it became quite clear Allen was looking for Moore early and often, and that the connection had grown quite well. The days of ‘everybody eats’ — their self-populated wide receiver mantra over the last two years in the post-Diggs era — have long since vanished with Moore on the team. There is now a genuine expectation Moore will be on the field all the time, giving the Bills a deep-field threat that simply did not exist in their offense the last two seasons.” — Joe Buscaglia
Last season: Byard not only performed at an All-Pro level, leading the NFL with seven interceptions, but he was also a tone-setting captain for the Bears and continued his iron man streak, upping his run of consecutive regular-season games played to 164.
Why he departed: The Bears, in a quest to upgrade their speed on defense, chose to go younger with the signing of 27-year-old athletic safety Coby Bryant. Byard’s market ultimately didn’t crystallize the way many thought it might, and he reunited in New England with coach Mike Vrabel, whom he was with from 2018 to 2023 when both were with the Tennessee Titans.
Contract situation: Byard’s deal with the Patriots was for one season and $9 million.
The word from New England: “Between his stature in the league and his pre-existing relationship with Vrabel, Byard has quickly become the vocal leader of the Patriots’ defense.
“Does the 33-year-old safety still have the same speed of six years ago? Maybe not. But his ball skills are still off the charts and he’s been great about ensuring the Patriots are lined up properly, quickly grasping this new defense he’s in. It seems unlikely that he’ll match his seven interceptions of a year ago, but Byard looks like a solid starting safety who will be the vocal leader for a secondary that has a ton of talent.” — Chad Graff
Last season: While a groin injury sent Edmunds to injured reserve for four weeks late in the season, his overall productivity was solid for the defense. He totaled a team-high 112 tackles plus four interceptions, a sack and a fumble recovery.
Why he departed: While Edmunds was an asset to the Bears defense, the aim at Halas Hall was to get faster and cheaper at linebacker. So, in a move to clear $15 million in salary-cap space, the Bears released the ninth-year veteran in March. Four days later, he landed on his feet for coordinator Dennard Wilson’s defense.
Contract situation: Edmunds’ third NFL contract — three years, $36 million — came with $23.7 million guaranteed.
The word from New York: “Edmunds has been a perfect fit for the overhauled linebacker corps. The Giants desperately needed an upgrade at middle linebacker after having the worst run defense in the NFL last season. Time will tell if Edmunds can still play at a high level, but he has looked the part during training camp.
“Edmunds has flashed the ball skills in camp that have been an asset throughout his career. Throwing over the middle against Edmunds and 6-foot-4 Arvell Reese has been a challenge for quarterbacks all summer.
“Equally important, Edmunds stepped in as a leader from Day 1. He was one of eight players voted to the Giants’ leadership council by teammates. His presence has been especially valuable to Reese, who was the fifth pick in this year’s draft. Edmunds and Reese have played side by side at inside linebacker, with the veteran constantly communicating with the raw rookie.” — Dan Duggan
Last season: Wright was one of the surprise standouts in the Bears’ division championship run, contributing to the defense’s league-high 33 takeaways with five interceptions plus two forced fumbles and three recoveries.
Why he departed: Rather than bet on Wright repeating his ball production from 2025, the Bears chose to push their chips in on Tyrique Stevenson as their preferred starter opposite Jaylon Johnson.
Contract situation: Wright signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract with the Jets with $3.5 million guaranteed, a relatively low-risk investment.
The word from New York: “The Jets signed Wright largely for his ball skills on a defense that didn’t intercept any passes last season — and also because he fits the physical type of cornerback that coach Aaron Glenn prefers. The plan was for him to compete for a starting job opposite Brandon Stephens and it looked like he was the leader to win that job in the spring.
“Once the summer started, though, second-year corner Azareye’h Thomas got the first reps with the starters. Then Wright dealt with an injury that knocked him out for most of training camp and ultimately cost him a chance to legitimately push to start. Thomas is highly unproven and doesn’t have a history of forcing turnovers, so it’s still entirely possible Wright eventually gets another shot. But for now he’ll be more of a depth piece than someone who gets significant playing time.” — Zack Rosenblatt
Last season: In a contract season, Brisker answered the bell with his durability, playing in all 19 games during the regular season and playoffs. He was at his best in the Bears’ playoff loss to the Los Angeles Rams, totaling 14 tackles, a sack and two passes defensed.
Why he departed: Brisker was the second player Poles drafted in 2022, with the new…

title: Why Broncos' RJ Harvey can be wild card in Denver's quest for offensive breakthrough "He's becoming a complete back, three downs," offensive coordinator Davis Webb said, "and that's what he wants to be." Nick Kosmider 1
summary:

Ja’Quan McMillian’s takeaway in overtime of the divisional playoff game against the Buffalo Bills put Denver’s offense on the field at its own 20-yard line. The Broncos needed only a field goal to win the game, but they had already punted af
full_text:
RJ Harvey pulls in a pass under pressure from Packers linebacker Edgerrin Cooper during their preseason matchup. Isaiah J. Downing / Imagn Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — The acrobatic, jaw-dropping interception gave the Broncos a second chance, but work remained.
Ja’Quan McMillian’s takeaway in overtime of the divisional playoff game against the Buffalo Bills put Denver’s offense on the field at its own 20-yard line. The Broncos needed only a field goal to win the game, but they had already punted after a short drive to begin the extra period. In fact, the Broncos had either punted or turned the ball over on four of their previous five drives. A winning march didn’t feel inevitable as the offense took the field.
That changed when RJ Harvey, then a rookie running back playing in his first NFL playoff game, caught the ball in the flat on second-and-7. Real estate was limited, with linebacker Shaq Thompson closing to within a yard of Harvey at the time he caught the ball from quarterback Bo Nix. The play appeared destined for a modest gain, one that would set up a pressure-packed third down inside Denver’s own 30-yard line.
“When the ball is in my hands, I’ve got to make one guy miss all the time,” Harvey said. “I’ve got to make ’em miss. When it’s crunch time, I feel like that’s when I really come alive.”
With one dynamic cut, Harvey juked Thompson and then darted upfield . As two more defenders closed on either side of him, Harvey zoomed into the space between, powering through contact as he picked up the first down. By the time he was finally wrestled out of bounds, he had gained 24 yards, completely changing the complexion of the drive. A few minutes later, Wil Lutz kicked the chip-shot field goal that sent Denver to the AFC Championship Game.
The play was a microcosm of the ability Harvey showcased during his rookie season to turn small slivers of space into big plays. The Broncos believe it could also preview the increased role he could have as a receiver in Denver’s offense. Harvey caught 47 passes for 356 yards and five touchdowns last season — and added nine catches for 68 yards in two playoff games. That from a player who caught only 61 passes during his four-year college career at Central Florida and had a route tree that was more of a mesquite bush than a towering oak.
“He ran a bunch of wheel routes, but not anything with the complexity of what we do here,” running backs coach Lou Ayeni said. “… But we looked at the explosion and the playmaking ability, and we knew that he could be a guy who could help us in that area. And for me, personally, he’s a former quarterback. I remember this with David Montgomery when I recruited him (at Iowa State), and with Josh Jacobs; they were both high school quarterbacks. One thing quarterbacks do is catch the snap every play. They play catch every night. It’s the same thing with RJ. All those guys had great hands, and once I said that with RJ, I said, ‘He’s going to catch 50 balls.'”
Harvey’s next step is becoming the kind of consistent, dangerous weapon as a receiver that coach Sean Payton had at running back for so many prolific offensive seasons in New Orleans. Reggie Bush. Pierre Thomas. Darren Sproles. Alvin Kamara. The Saints, during Payton’s 16-year tenure as head coach, ranked first in running back receiving yards seven times, according to TruMedia. They finished second three other times and ranked fourth once. The Broncos, across three seasons since Payton became head coach, rank ninth in receiving yards among running backs, but only 30th in yards per reception.
Harvey could help lift both figures this season. Some of that will come simply from familiarity with Denver’s offense. Ayeni noted that Harvey came from a system at UCF that featured a handful of one-word play calls, many of which had the same result: give the ball to the All-American running back. The playbook was far more verbose when Harvey arrived in Denver as a second-round pick.
“There were more concepts in our first install than he probably had in his whole life,” Ayeni said. “Once he got comfortable, we wanted to be able to move him around and do different things where we can get him more involved in the passing game, get him out of the backfield where we can utilize him in matchups with linebackers and maybe even safeties. We knew we were going to add more to his plate. It was just a matter of time with him being ready.”
His preseason touchdown against the Packers last month demonstrated an improved route-running ability heading into his second season. He has a deeper grasp of the philosophy behind Denver’s concepts, allowing the running back, in his words, to “feel a lot more comfortable.” Harvey used a quick fake to make Packers linebacker Edgerrin Cooper take a step inside, then burned past Cooper as he ran up the sideline. Harvey adjusted for Nix’s throw, leaping up at the front of the end zone and holding onto the ball through contact.
Harvey spent ample time with Nix this offseason. He joined Nix, Denver’s other quarterbacks and many of the team’s receivers in Austin, Texas, in June for a player-organized passing camp. As Nix was completing his rehab from ankle surgery ahead of the start of camp, Harvey was there to catch his passes during late-summer throwing sessions.
“You can feel that there’s just a connection with those two,” Ayeni said, “and hopefully that will be a great connection for a long time here in Denver.”
That chemistry was already on display between Nix and Harvey during the latter’s rookie season, highlighted by a touchdown connection between the two that cemented a late-season victory in Kansas City. The Broncos faced a third-and-goal at the Chiefs’ 1-yard line, the game tied coming out of the 2-minute warning. Nix darted to his right at the snap as Harvey ran a flat route toward the front pylon. Chiefs safety Bryan Cook shadowed Harvey as he reached the end zone. Still, as he caught Nix’s eyes turning him inside, the running back abruptly stopped his route, freeing himself just enough from Cook’s coverage to become an open target of the quarterback’s game-winning touchdown pass.
“For a rookie, it was a pretty instinctive play,” Payton said, “and you would’ve guessed it would’ve been a (wide) receiver.”
The Broncos enter this season with perhaps the most complete running back room since Payton became the team’s head coach. Veteran J.K. Dobbins is healthy entering the season and figures to be Denver’s lead ball-carrier so long as he is on the field. The Broncos should endeavor not to have Dobbins occupy 73 percent of running back carries, as he did last season before his Week 10 foot injury. But rookie Jonah Coleman also appears ready for a featured role as a runner. Harvey brings an explosive element as a runner — he had three carries for at least 38 yards last season — and first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb said near the end of camp that Harvey is “tremendously improved” as a runner after a rookie season in which he averaged 3.7 yards per rush.
“He’s becoming a complete back, three downs,” Webb said, “and that’s what he wants to be.”
The task for Webb this season: find more ways to put Harvey in situations to “make ’em miss.”

title: Gauging where Packers fans' optimism level should be heading into season: Mailbag The Packers enter the 2026 season with plenty of talent but also plenty of questions. Matt Schneidman 12
summary:

GREEN BAY, Wis. — The Green Bay Packers will play a football game that matters nine days from Friday.
To pass the time until then, indulge in this mailbag. All of your great questions were appreciated.
Is it just me, or were you more impressed with what you saw from Dani Dennis-Sutton in a quarter than Barryn Sorrell in the first two games? — @joeypetersen8
Sorrell pl
full_text:
Matt LaFleur heads into his eighth season as Packers head coach, coming off a 9-7-1 campaign in 2025. Mark Hoffman / Imagn Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — The Green Bay Packers will play a football game that matters nine days from Friday.
To pass the time until then, indulge in this mailbag. All of your great questions were appreciated.
Is it just me, or were you more impressed with what you saw from Dani Dennis-Sutton in a quarter than Barryn Sorrell in the first two games? — @joeypetersen8
Sorrell played 11 total snaps in the first two preseason games, according to Pro Football Focus. Dennis-Sutton was playing against backups in the finale, his lone preseason game. Context is important. Why did Sorrell play that little and then not suit up for the third game? Because of how he played throughout a month of camp practices. It’s not just about the games on TV when evaluating players at this time of year, especially when those games are exhibitions.
What does the offensive line look like if Zach Bako-Bewele and/or Aaron Banks can’t go against Minnesota? — @97Jaeger11
I think both guys will play, but my takeaway from the Packers’ recent messaging on both is that they want to see Bako-Bewele and Banks play consistently coming off injuries before speaking more confidently about them. Anthony Belton is the backup right tackle and Jager Burton is the backup left guard.
As a loyal fan since 1989, why should I be optimistic that this year will be any different from last year or the past several years, where in critical situations, this team under Matt LaFleur melts down and breaks our hearts? — @RyanWalters2519
You want my honest opinion? I don’t think it will be much different. Not necessarily from the back-breaking collapses perspective, but from the overall record and playoff finish perspective. I’m skeptical of the pass rush without Micah Parsons and the cornerback room. I’m skeptical of the offensive line, which has performance or health questions at four of five spots. I’m skeptical of the backfield without Josh Jacobs. The Packers have talent, but that’s too many questions for me to think they can take a big step forward.
What’s a realistic number of touches that you think MarShawn Lloyd will get per game? He seems to be all we really got, but surely the staff won’t want to give him too much to risk injury? — @RobLorge
Matt LaFleur said Lloyd’s workload is to be determined, while Lloyd himself said he’s ready for whatever. There’s no way they load him up with 20 carries next Sunday, but maybe they gradually get there if Lloyd proves he can stay healthy while handling a slightly lighter workload to start the season (and if Josh Jacobs is still out). Lloyd averaged barely more than 10 carries per game in his last year at USC and hasn’t been a high-volume guy since high school. It would be malpractice if the Packers made him one from the jump, especially considering his injury history.
Who will have a bigger impact on the offense early (first quarter of the season), Jonnu Smith or Kaleb Johnson? — @John_G_16
I’ll go with Smith. His experience in both the NFL and iterations of this offense will probably allow him to contribute more right away. Johnson played in a similar system last year in Pittsburgh, but he’s only in his second year while Smith is in Year 10. I also think Smith’s skill set lends itself better to early production than Johnson’s. General manager Brian Gutekunst sounded enamored with Smith’s repertoire. He might be the No. 2 tight end by Week 1 and can catch passes downfield, which is important considering Tucker Kraft is really the only proven one doing that among the tight ends. Johnson might be more of a pass-protecting back to start the season, and that’s fine. I don’t see him touching the ball all that much right out of the gate.
Is everyone actually content going into this season with this CB room? — @MichaelFitqnik
If by everyone you mean the fanbase, I would say no. And I would agree with you all. The Packers’ No. 1 corner, according to how they’ve lined up in practice, is a rookie who’s about to line up across from Justin Jefferson at times in his NFL debut. Keisean Nixon will probably be the other starter alongside Brandon Cisse, and Nixon needs to prove he can play like he did in the first half of last season and not the second. Carrington Valentine has plenty of starting experience and is a solid No. 3, if that’s where he is on the depth chart, and Benjamin St-Juste also brings valuable experience if he needs to play. If Parsons were healthy, I don’t think people would be as concerned with this group because they wouldn’t have to cover for as long. But the Packers’ potential shortcomings at cornerback are at risk of being exposed without a formidable pass rush.
Is MLF really going to let Jordan Love cook this year? — @MarkKnowsItAll
I definitely think the Packers need to be a pass-heavy team. They obviously need at least a decent dose of running to keep defenses somewhat on their toes, but what would you rather rely on if you’re LaFleur: Love, Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, Jayden Reed and Kraft or Lloyd and Chris Brooks? The answer is obvious, but it’s also a moot point if the offensive line doesn’t block for either the run or the pass. Some of those aforementioned questions up front — Jordan Morgan’s performance at a new position, Jacob Monk’s readiness as a starter and the health of Bako-Bewele and Banks — need positive answers for the offense to unlock its full potential.
Do you still want LaFleur fired? — @Garm1981
I shouldn’t even give questions like this the time of day, but I can’t help myself. I’ll make this abundantly clear one last time. My line of questioning to LaFleur after the Eagles game last season was based on something I heard from inside the building, not my own opinion that he should be on the hot seat. There’s a big difference between reporting what’s happening and writing my opinion. In fact, I wrote later in the season that LaFleur deserved an extension. That was my opinion. I don’t *want* anything. I’m not a fan and I don’t let my personal opinions of people impact how I cover them. And it’s not like I raised this topic out of thin air. Team president Ed Policy himself opened that door by not extending LaFleur before last season and saying he didn’t like lame-duck years. But if you’d like to persist with the narrative that I was trying to get LaFleur fired, go right ahead.
Is Chris Brooks the No. 3 now behind Kaleb Johnson? — @MeloVader916
Not yet, I don’t think. Once Johnson grasps the offense and gets his feet wet in games for the Packers, I wouldn’t be surprised if he leaps Brooks on the depth chart. Johnson has more upside with the ball in his hands than Brooks. We pretty much know what Brooks is at this point: a great pass protector who’s efficient with the ball in his hands in small doses. That fits the role of a No. 3 back, but the Packers would love to unlock the potential that made Johnson a third-round pick a year ago so he can complement Lloyd better (if Jacobs remains out).
One position group that got stronger, one group that got weaker? — @adproh
I think the quarterback position got weaker. That was always going to happen since the Packers weren’t paying Malik Willis in free agency. He was probably the NFL’s best backup. Now, they have a backup in Tyrod Taylor, whom they trust to run the offense and hold his own if Love goes down since he’s seen everything in this league, but Taylor doesn’t have the upside of Willis and probably can’t win you a game like Willis could. I think the interior defensive line has gotten stronger since last season ended. Not only is Devonte Wyatt healthy, but Javon Hargrave still has some juice left and Warren Brinson looks to have made a big Year 2 jump. Rookie third-rounder Chris McClellan also showed in the preseason why he could see spot snaps immediately, especially since defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon will rotate those guys more than Jeff Hafley…

title: How to watch the Los Angeles Chargers: Schedule, TV info for Justin Herbert's Bolts Justin Herbert and Jim Harbaugh look to build on consecutive 11-6 seasons. Here's how to tune in for all 17 games in 2026. Steven Louis Goldstein 1
summary:

It never rains in Southern California, as Albert Hammond (and Raphael Saadiq ) insisted. But, just this one time, can lightning strike in Inglewood?
With Justin Herbert in the pocket and Jim Harbaugh on the headset, the Los Angeles Chargers have put together back-to-back 11-6 efforts. It’s been a respectable run, but both of those seasons ended in dispiriting wild-card knockouts. Is a powder-blue breakout
full_text:
Justin Herbert arrives on the heels of consecutive 11-win seasons. Harry How / Getty Images
It never rains in Southern California, as Albert Hammond (and Raphael Saadiq ) insisted. But, just this one time, can lightning strike in Inglewood?
With Justin Herbert in the pocket and Jim Harbaugh on the headset, the Los Angeles Chargers have put together back-to-back 11-6 efforts. It’s been a respectable run, but both of those seasons ended in dispiriting wild-card knockouts. Is a powder-blue breakout in the cards for 2026? Can the “ Super Chargers ” actually push for a Super Bowl, one in their home stadium at that?
Herbert’s returning targets include chain-mover Ladd McConkey and field-stretcher Quentin Johnston. He also has two new tight ends in Charlie Kolar and David Njoku. Running back Omarion Hampton, a 2025 first-round draft pick, returns from an injury-shortened rookie season with considerable upside. And the whole offense should get some much-needed protection if tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt are healthy again. Let’s see what new coordinator Mike McDaniel can do with a clean slate.
L.A.’s defense fields an electric front between Pro Bowl edge rusher Tuli Tuipulotu, hometown favorite Daiyan Henley, hyped-up rookie Akheem Mesidor and likely Hall of Famer Khalil Mack. As usual, Derwin James Jr. captains the secondary. While former defensive coordinator Jesse Minter is now leading the Baltimore Ravens, successor Chris O’Leary takes on a group that ranked No. 5 in yards allowed and No. 9 in scoring D last season.
The Chargers are set for three primetime matchups this fall, plus late-season flex games against the rival Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos. Use this guide below to refresh on the national TV rotation, plus the streaming restrictions for in- and out-of-market fans. Follow both the team itself and beat writer Daniel Popper on The Athletic .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with former Chargers quarterback Drew Brees. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.

title: Why the Rams are placing a greater emphasis on special teams this season Entering a season with high expectations, the Rams made their special teams units more of a priority after the many miscues in 2025. Nate Atkins 5
summary:
The Rams' special teams units had their share of challenges during a 2025 season in which they were one win from reaching the Super Bowl. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Rams are seven months from two muffed punts in the NFC Championship Game, a blocked punt in the wild-card round, a season of blocked field goals and penalties and explosive punt returns allowed by a special teams phase they left to the bottom of a top-heavy roster, only to pay for it when the lights wer
full_text:
The Rams' special teams units had their share of challenges during a 2025 season in which they were one win from reaching the Super Bowl. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Rams are seven months from two muffed punts in the NFC Championship Game, a blocked punt in the wild-card round, a season of blocked field goals and penalties and explosive punt returns allowed by a special teams phase they left to the bottom of a top-heavy roster, only to pay for it when the lights were brightest.
It started with a coordinator switch. It was followed by a couple of signings that fell way below the radar in an offseason headlined by Matthew Stafford’s return for an 18th season and blockbuster trades for All-Pro defenders Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie .
As Super Bowl favorites with a ticking clock on Stafford’s career, the Rams weren’t oblivious when the margins began screaming to them on special teams.
“I’m not going to run away (from the fact) that I haven’t done a good enough job of making that an emphasis,” coach Sean McVay said. “It’s cost us, and that is nobody’s fault but my own.”
This roster, this leadership, this system, this practice plan — it all had to be different than it was a year ago.
“We could be the reason why we win a game,” linebacker Shaun Dolac said, “but we don’t want to be the reason why we lose.”
Last season went so off the rails on special teams, with mistakes offering daggers in nearly all of their six losses, that the Rams did something rarely seen from a team with a playoff spot locked up: They fired a coordinator with two games to go.
After dismissing Chase Blackburn, they did their best to patch things together with interim coordinator Ben Kotwica. They eliminated some penalty issues, and the kicking game continued to improve. But they couldn’t prevent some moments that defined their playoff run, from the blocked punt in the final minutes against the Carolina Panthers in the wild-card round to Xavier Smith’s two muffed punts against the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC championship.
It all led to one of the most important moves McVay would have to make this offseason in hiring new special teams coaches. He ultimately landed on a tandem in coordinator Bubba Ventrone and assistant Kyle Hoke, both from the Cleveland Browns. It was a bet on the pair to rebound from some miscues that sunk the Browns’ season last year — and to get back to the levels Ventrone has shown before.
Ventrone was considered a rising star during his tenure as coordinator with the Indianapolis Colts from 2018 to 2022. His units regularly created explosive returns, blocked punts, blocked field goals and were precise in flipping field position. His process was to develop players from special-teamers into offensive and defensive starters who kept their third-phase focus. He hit on names such as All-Pro Ashton Dulin and Pro Bowlers Zaire Franklin and Kenny Moore II.
The development plan would have to be different on a team with immediate goals. But what still exists is Ventrone’s intensity and pedigree as a coordinator with eight years of experience and as a player who lasted a decade as one of the most physical and vocal special-teamers, including for four years under Bill Belichick with the New England Patriots.
“Bubba came in and showed his personality, he showed us who he is as a coach, and he’s been doing it for a long time as a player as well,” Dolac said. “He brings that intensity every single day into the meetings, and we love that from him. You get it every day from him.
“He does a good job being just a teacher, teaching us how to do things. We have the ability to ask questions, and he has the answers to every question that we have.”
A new voice in the room was one shift. But it would only matter if the players he coached were up to the challenge.
For all of last year’s special teams nightmares, the Rams felt they at least had a kicking game to bring back.
Ethan Evans had some electric punts last season, including the 50-yard boot against the Seahawks that landed at the 1-yard line in Week 11 to help seal a 21-19 win.
Harrison Mevis became a revelation after his midseason replacement of Joshua Karty, who kept falling victim to blocked kicks in addition to some misses. Between the regular season and playoffs, Mevis delivered on every extra point as well as 18 of 19 field goals, including a 42-yard game winner in the snow to beat the Chicago Bears in the divisional round.
But Evans’ second-half regression, and all of the issues that compounded in penalties and returns allowed and blocked kicks in crunch time, magnified a glaring issue in the foundation: The Rams were trusting too many young players on special teams. They tried to rectify it at midseason by bringing back 38-year-old long snapper Jake McQuaide. But what became clear was that a special teams unit that relied largely on first- and second-year players was doomed on the biggest stages against the best opponents.
So, the Rams went after two veterans in free agency: long snapper Joe Cardona and cover man Grant Stuard. Cardona, now in his 12th season, played his first three for Ventrone in New England. Stuard, now in his sixth season, spent a year with Ventrone in 2022 in Indianapolis after Ventrone sought him out in a trade from the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
The Ventrone relationship would mean plenty once Stuard was on the practice field cracking teammates, taking them to the ground and barking back at his coaches.
“If I say something to him or he bites at me, we’re familiar with each other,” Stuard said of Ventrone. “There’s no distaste.”
It has empowered Stuard to take charge of the goal he had when signing with the Rams, which was to become the leader of a special teams unit.
“Me as a player can be an acquired taste,” Stuard said. “… If you hate it, oh well, I’ll go somewhere else.”
The Rams have welcomed it, because they know that after last year, they aren’t in a spot to reject alternatives. In one practice, Stuard went at it with offensive coordinator Nathan Scheelhaase, who got on him about taking players to the ground. At one point in training camp, McVay came out to Stuard to talk him into a more middle-ground approach. But it wasn’t a rejection of his persona in a year with so much on the line.
That doesn’t mean everything changed. The Rams made a bold choice in bringing Smith back after he muffed the two punts in Seattle. They’ve worked with him to grow from it and were encouraged when he returned a 40-yard punt in the preseason opener against the Kansas City Chiefs.
“It’s not about how you react but about how you respond to those adversity situations,” Smith said, echoing a message McVay shares all the time.
The Rams spent the majority of their training camp practices at Loyola Marymount University with a new approach: They began the day on special teams.
“It gives us a way to start off practice, and you can emphasize starting fast on special teams, which will then translate to how we practice the rest of the day,” running back Ronnie Rivers said.
Added Dolac, “We’re all just going at 100 miles an hour and making sure the younger guys see it. That’s the standard around here.”
They are playing more offensive and defensive players on special teams, including Konata Mumpfield, Tyler Higbee, Nate Landman and Kam Kinchens .
“You have guys who are starters on offense or defense who are in Year 11, 12, guys like Higbee who are going out there and giving great effort and who are concerned with doing the right stuff when that’s not conditional upon them making the team,” Stuard said. “He can suck on punt, but he’s going to be out there in 13 personnel. The collective wants to be good. It’s not, ‘What can I do to be available?’ It’s, ‘How can I make this unit better?’”
They all feel the weight of what went wrong last year. That’s true for a player with a second chance like Smith and a newcomer like Stuard, who isn’t afraid to push the boundaries McVay has in practice.

title: A rocket scientist quit SpaceX to pursue football. Now he's the Vikings' secret weapon Chenzo Funari may have a non-traditional football background, but his brains and attitude have made him incredibly valuable to the Vikings. Alec Lewis 32
summary:
Vikings assistant defensive backs coach Chenzo Funari has a shockingly non-traditional football background. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; photos: Kara Durrette, Stephen Maturen, David McNew / Getty Images
To tell this preposterous tale appropriately, we must begin in the Mojave Desert.

full_text:
Vikings assistant defensive backs coach Chenzo Funari has a shockingly non-traditional football background. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; photos: Kara Durrette, Stephen Maturen, David McNew / Getty Images
To tell this preposterous tale appropriately, we must begin in the Mojave Desert.
Perceptions do the place justice. Jagged mountains break up the burnt orange landscape. Outposts surface along Route 66. Live here for a time, and there is a high probability your background would sound straight out of a novel.
Such was the case for Chenzo Funari, now the Minnesota Vikings’ assistant defensive backs coach.
In the fall of 2015, Funari lived in the desert of Southern California as part of an internship with the aerospace company Masten Space Systems. He worked for months in a World War II-era garage.
“We went out and tested small rocket engines,” Funari, 32, said after a recent Vikings practice. “Blew stuff up.”
In those days, Funari’s sister, Taylor, periodically checked his location on her iPhone. The dot zig-zagged across areas of the American West that are not even marked on maps by city names.
“I would text him and be, like, ‘Why are you in the middle of nowhere?’” she said. “And he would reply with, ‘We’re testing. A rocket just combusted.’ And I would think to myself, ‘Is that bad? Are you OK? What does that mean?’”
Time at Masten launched Funari’s wildly impressive first career. In 2017, he helped develop an injector for a rocket at Blue Origin, a company determined to transport humans to space. In 2019, following a master’s program at Purdue, SpaceX hired him to contribute his expertise to their “Raptor” engine, intended to bring people to Mars.
Funari had arguably reached the pinnacle of a highly competitive industry before age 30. And then, in 2020, undeterred by the astonishment from colleagues and family members, he withdrew from that life entirely.
“I’ll never forget the day I got the call from him,” his mother, Kim, said. “I’m in the car, and I pick up the phone, and he goes, ‘Mom, I’m quitting my job at SpaceX to pursue football.”
This audacious decision paved the way for the present.
Funari turned a volunteer coaching opportunity at Youngstown State into a meaningful role on one of the most respected defensive staffs in the NFL. Now, staffers and players rave about his digestible understanding of schematic trends and his impact on advanced scouting reports.
His journey represents possibility and a disregard for convention. The same forces that led Funari to the Mojave Desert brought him to Minnesota. He chased his passions with intensity, only to realize along the way the one that put him most at peace.
As a child, Funari fixated on two things: space and sports.
He studied constellations. At the dinner table, he quizzed his parents on the solar system. Taylor still doesn’t know the answer to a question he’d constantly pose when he entered the living room: What is the average temperature on Mars?
“It was like he was a walking encyclopedia,” she said.
The Cleveland native also adored the playing style of Hall of Fame quarterback Brett Favre. Maybe it was the fearlessness, possibly the flair. Funari practiced youth football with the gunslinger on his mind. His parents quickly recognized the sport was one of the few activities that gave his brain a break.
His mother enjoyed nothing more than watching her son, spent, plop onto the couch after another evening playing under the lights.
“As a parent, I realized that I had a profound responsibility for this kid,” Kim said. “His mind never shut off, and it brought a kind of electricity and friction into our home. Ideas sparking. Questions multiplying. His ambitions formed long before any other kid knew what that word meant. Sports, though, were where his mind went quiet.”
To his family, Funari needed the camaraderie of competition. That’s what made his torn right ACL as a ninth-grader so demoralizing.
At the pre-operation appointment for the initial repair, Funari informed his mother that his left knee also throbbed. The doctors diagnosed him with a microfracture resulting from stress applied by playing football with the torn ACL in his right knee.
He recovered from both injuries, only to tear his ACL again in his junior year. Another surgeon suggested that a reconstruction could return him to the field in eight months, but that the procedure could jeopardize his future ability to walk.
“I mean, I saw a human being’s spirit break in that room when they told us that,” Kim said. “It was so detrimental.”
Funari quit football for a season, but the high school coaches reeled him back in with a coaching assistant role. The team connectivity rekindled his love of the game.
If it weren’t for his time commitment to studying aeronautical and astronautical engineering at Ohio State, Funari would have assisted with the Buckeyes’ football program.
“As a 17-year-old, I figured the engineering degree was probably the smarter choice,” Funari said. “So, I decided to do that.”
Masten and Blue Origin gave him hands-on time with propulsion and combustion devices. He wrote code. He helped assemble products. These lessons piqued the interest of the Zucrow Laboratories at Purdue, the world’s largest academic propulsion lab.
There, as part of his studies, he assisted on a project funded by SpaceX and the Air Force.
Exposure to SpaceX earned him a full-time job with the company, where he worked on the engine for the “Starship” rocket. At the time, Funari lived in El Segundo, Calif. His sister lived in Hollywood. They planned to see each other often, but his work made that difficult.
This wore on him, and he couldn’t stop ruminating over several questions: Am I satisfied with what I’m doing? Am I bought into SpaceX’s mission the way others are? Can I live the life I want to live by continuing down this path?
While at home for Christmas that winter, he scavenged through some old pamphlets in his room and found a paper he’d written in elementary school.
“And it was, ‘What are the three things for me to have a successful life?’” Funari said. “I had written: have a family, graduate from college and be a football coach. What brought me fulfillment was the relationships with the game. I couldn’t get the thought out of my head.”
In the fall of 2020, during the pandemic, Youngstown State allowed its football staff to post a volunteer job opening. More than 100 people applied almost immediately.
“I told one of our young coaches, ‘Go through that stack of resumes, and bring me something if you see anything that catches your eye,’” Joe Schaefer, then the school’s defensive coordinator, said.
An hour later, the young coach walked into his office with a wry smile.
“I’m, like, ‘What’s so funny?’” Schaefer recalled.
He grabbed the document containing Funari’s resume.
“I knew I had to call the guy,” Schaefer said. “Like, right then and there.”
Funari accepted the phone call. They exchanged pleasantries, then Schaefer cut to the chase.
Why on earth would you do this?
Funari’s family shared the same incredulity when he first told them of his decision. However, they understood that his hunger for success pushed the boundaries of others’ beliefs, and they saw the flicker of football throughout his upbringing.
Schaefer heard the emotion in his voice. Funari validated the commitment by packing his car and arriving at the school the next day.
“As his younger sister, watching him do that fueled me so much,” Taylor said. “I had just graduated college. The job market was terrible. I wanted to work in music, and he made me feel like that was realistic. There’s nothing he does that he hasn’t thought about completely. He has this sense of knowing.”
As part of his many responsibilities at Youngstown, he analyzed data sets to gather intel on upcoming opponents. He delivered the insights in a clear, coherent way. His efficiency made it likely that he would find advantages to exploit.
Word of his influence spread throughout coaching…

Defensive coordinator Brandon Staley returns, with his defense coming off a second-half surge last year. Saints staple Cameron Jordan is back for his 16th season with the franchise. He and Chase Young teamed up for 20 1/2 sacks in 2025 and will try to pick up where they left off. However, the absence of Bryan Bresee is sure to be felt after the defensive tackle tore his ACL in training camp.
New Orleans looks like one of the league’s more intriguing stories, but with streaming deals and a growing supply of international games, knowing when and where to watch your team is more difficult than ever. With that in mind, we’ve compiled a guide to get you through all 17 regular-season matchups.
Make sure you’re following the Saints on The Athletic . Scoop City delivers updates from around the NFL, “ The Athletic Football Show ” breaks down the league in depth, and the national staff covers everything from power rankings and fantasy football to injuries, transactions and feature reporting.
All times listed below are ET.

It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.

RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
