Harbaugh is in his first year with the Giants and also the co-founder of th
full_text:
John Harbaugh is in his first season as the New York Giants' head coach. Illustration: Dan Goldfarb / The Athletic; AP Photo / Seth Wenig
Peak newsletter 🧠 | This is an excerpt from The Athletic’s weekly newsletter covering the mental side of sports. Sign up here to receive the Peak newsletter directly in your inbox.
Every month, New York Giants coach John Harbaugh will answer reader-submitted questions about leadership.
Harbaugh is in his first year with the Giants and also the co-founder of the Harbaugh Coaching Academy , a non-profit that helps coaches at all levels.
Anyone interested in asking Harbaugh a question about leadership can submit one in the box below. You can read last month’s Q&A here .
When dealing with a subordinate (player or coach) who feels as if they have earned an opportunity you can’t give them, how do you navigate that? — Cole K.
Harbaugh: Just with honesty. I’ve had those conversations here in the last few days.
I think most of these guys deserve more of an opportunity than they’re actually getting because the competition is so tough. So many times the key to making it is just the chance to break through. Getting that chance is not always easy.
I just try to explain the circumstances: “Here is where we’re at. This is where we stand and how you fit into that.”
I try to acknowledge the fact that they deserve more; they’ve earned more. I tell guys: “You should be on this 53-man roster. You should be on another 53. You deserve to be on a 53-man roster. But this is why it’s not working out here right now.”
Do you coach an established star and an undrafted rookie the same way? And why? — Pierre B.
Harbaugh: I don’t think you coach any two people the same way. Everybody is unique. Nobody is the same.
You don’t categorize them as an established star or an unestablished player or whatever. It’s more about: Who is this person? I try to have as many conversations with the unestablished player as I do with the star player.
The conversations are different because they’re different people, and what they need and where they’re at is different.
I try to think of them individually more than I do categorically.
As a young coach, my biggest struggle is knowing early on whether a player responds to hard coaching or a softer touch. What tangible signs do you look for to figure that out fast, instead of learning through trial and error? — Jack D.
Harbaugh: So interesting, but I don’t know if I would define it like that. How would you define what a softer touch is and what hard coaching is? What does that mean exactly?
It probably means different things to different people, so I think you have to be careful about that.
To me, start with yourself first. Check your own heart.
Yeah, I want to be pragmatic, I want to be utilitarian, I want to find the best way to reach the player to get the most out of them. But I have to check myself first. What is my motivation? Is my motivation that I want to win a bunch of games? Yeah, of course. But it should be more about the player themself.
What’s best for this player? What can I do to help this player be the best version of themself? Why are we here? What’s the end goal?
Teachers should be about students; coaches should be about players first.
And then the next thing is: Meet the person where they’re at. Try to build a relationship with that person. What would it take to gain their trust in a way that they understand that you have their best interest at heart and you want what’s best for them?
It’s not about hard coaching or soft coaching. It’s more about relatable coaching.
How do you handle tough conversations? Telling someone they are cut, not starting, having to fire someone, etc.? — Bryton S.
Harbaugh: All of that should start from an empathetic place. You want to put yourself in the other person’s shoes. I’ve been in those shoes, too.
I try to do it in a way that’s positive, and I try to put it in perspective in terms of all the great things they’re doing. I just try to explain the situation and the circumstances for what they are.
And if there are some things they can do better, you want to be honest and forthright about those things in a positive way.
Many leaders share how they’ve held subordinates accountable. How have you held peers accountable? What are those challenges with peers? — Tom S.
Harbaugh: That’s a great question. As coaches, we’re all peers, but even at this pro level, you are, in a sense, a peer — partner is probably a better word — with your players.
Players and coaches are partnered in the mission of putting the best team out there. And they’re also partnered to help each other achieve their goals, ambitions and dreams.
I think you do it by holding each other accountable in a relationship kind of way. Like, I care about you. If somebody is willing to take the risk to come to me and tell me that I can do something better, then I shouldn’t be defensive about that. I should look at that from the perspective of: This person really cares about me and wants to help me.
That gives the other person permission to come to you and help you be better.
It’s a lot easier to not say anything.
If we can all understand that that’s the perspective we’re coming from, then I think you can relate to everybody that way, your peers as well.
What would be your advice for a young athlete trying to be a leader on their own team? And how would you say your leadership on the playing field translates to life skills? — Nico
Harbaugh: It absolutely translates. Football or any other sport, to me, is a metaphor for life. There are teams everywhere. Your family is a team. You’re on a team, man, and you’re facing life’s challenges together.
Your first job, you’re on a team, and you need to be a great teammate.
First of all, great leadership starts with being a great teammate and a great server. What leaders do is help everybody around them be better. The best leaders, guys like Ray Lewis and Ed Reed, made all the other players and coaches better because of how they did their job and operated.
And then you actually have to care about the people who are looking to you for leadership. You have to put them first. They’ve got to know that you really, really care about them, that you’re in their corner, and you want them to do well.
The other thing is the example you set. You’ve got to be willing to get in there and do the work. You’ve got to be willing to get in there and make the same sacrifices that you’re asking the people around you to make.
How do you move your players beyond what they believe is possible when you’re the one holding the vision? I’m curious about the balance between what they want for themselves and what you want for them. — Christina J.
Harbaugh: Ah, such a great point. It’s really important to blend, marry and intertwine the individual dreams and goals with the team mission. Those two things need to go together.
We fully acknowledge that our players have dreams and goals and aspirations, and we want to be there for them to realize all of those things.
We encourage our players and coaches to rally behind one another: Tell us what your dreams are. Tell us what your goals are. Tell us a dream that you’re really afraid to speak publicly because you’re afraid someone is going to make fun of it.
We want to know how big your dream is because we want to help you get there.
There actually is an “I” in team. Matter of fact, on our team there are 53 “I”s, and there are a lot more as part of the broader team and organization. And all of the “I”s are working together to create the team.
You have to take into account those individual aspirations and try to focus and blend them all together.
How have you motivated your own players to grow into leadership roles on your teams? — Rene R.
Harbaugh: Some people just aren’t as comfortable getting up in front of the room and speaking. Some people are just a little more reserved. That’s OK. You can lead within that personality type.
A lot of those guys, when they…

title: Gauging John Harbaugh's impact and what to expect in Week 1: Giants mailbag Dan Duggan 7
summary:
Under John Harbaugh, the Giants look unquestionably better prepared to begin the season than in the recent past. Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The New York Giants are enjoying a four-day break after a grueling training camp, with preparations for the Sept. 13 season opener against the Dallas Cowboys shifting into high gear Monday. But interest in this team never rests, so the mailbag was full as we try to bridge the gap to get closer to kicking off the John Harbaugh era.
full_text:
Under John Harbaugh, the Giants look unquestionably better prepared to begin the season than in the recent past. Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The New York Giants are enjoying a four-day break after a grueling training camp, with preparations for the Sept. 13 season opener against the Dallas Cowboys shifting into high gear Monday. But interest in this team never rests, so the mailbag was full as we try to bridge the gap to get closer to kicking off the John Harbaugh era.
(Editor’s note: Questions have been edited for clarity.)
What do you think John Harbaugh’s biggest impact has been? — Steven K.
Harbaugh has brought credibility to the organization. No one knows if this will ultimately work. Plenty of accomplished coaches have flamed out at later stops. But no other coach on the market this offseason could have generated this level of buy-in. A leader with a clear vision is leading the organization. Everyone believes in Harbaugh’s methods because he can point to his lengthy track record of success. The Giants feel like a professional organization for the first time in a long time. How that translates to wins and losses remains to be seen, but Harbaugh’s impact has already been profound.
What are the vibes you’re getting from Harbaugh and the team as we approach Week 1? — Pat D.
To Harbaugh’s credit: confidence. It used to drive me crazy at this time of year when general manager Joe Schoen and former coach Brian Daboll always ran from any expectation of winning games. That’s what made Harbaugh’s comments Wednesday about expecting to win so refreshing. Surely there has to be some anxiety about starting this new journey with a roster that clearly has flaws. But Harbaugh and the players seem genuinely eager to get started.
It’s been apparent that the Giants were never ready for Week 1 under the last few head coaches. After what seemed to be a grueling John Harbaugh training camp, can you say with confidence that this team is prepared to compete on “Sunday Night Football” against a division rival and get a win? — Hasib H.
The common thread to the slow starts has mostly been bad teams. But it’s impossible to ignore how poorly the Giants have come out of the gate in recent seasons. They’ve been outscored 89-12 in their past three openers. Harbaugh has mostly been successful in openers, although he lost his last two in Baltimore.
The Giants are unquestionably better prepared this year. It’s not just the hard practices. It’s also the heightened emphasis on situational football and attention to detail. Now, none of that guarantees a win against the Cowboys in Week 1. Dallas has a better team on paper. But the Giants have a chance to prove otherwise on “Sunday Night Football.”
What schematically should we expect to see from the new offense compared with previous seasons? — Chris H.
Chris’ full question included the words “ground-and-pound,” and that’s a fitting description. Making 300-pound Pat Ricard the highest-paid fullback in the league was a clear signal of the offensive identity. The Giants spent a ton of time drilling quarterback Jaxson Dart on play-action passes from under center, which is designed to build off their power run game. Wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely add a dynamic element to the offense, but expect the Giants to seek explosives in the pass game after grinding teams on the ground. Don’t expect a wide-open passing attack.
Should there be any concerns with so many “chefs in the kitchen” when it comes to the offense? Between Greg Roman, Brian Callahan and Matt Nagy, you have a lot of voices. Will there be enough cohesion for Jaxson Dart to be successful? — Chris S.
This is a valid question, and it’s obviously too soon to answer definitively. Everyone has been saying the right things. But it’s unconventional to have Nagy as the play caller needing to fit in with a bunch of assistants he has no history with. I’m curious how that will come together. The optimistic view is the Giants have many coaches with loads of experience, so if they put their egos aside, they can tap into a deep reservoir of ideas and knowledge.
The upcoming draft is thought to be a “generational” QB draft. Given that Dart was “Daboll’s guy,” do you think there will be any pressure on his performance this year with the crop of new QBs who could be drafted? — Michael D.
Harbaugh had options this offseason, so one can make the case that Dart became his guy when he chose the Giants. The answer to these questions always comes from how the player and team perform. It wasn’t long ago that Daniel Jones was facing a make-or-break season in the first year under Schoen and Daboll. Jones performed well and the Giants won in 2022, so he cashed in. He was at another crossroads in 2024. Jones and the team flopped, so the Giants moved on to Dart.
If the Giants are bad enough that they’re in the Arch Manning sweepstakes, that means Dart — assuming he’s healthy — will have played poorly enough for them to be open to moving on. There’s no added pressure on Dart. He simply needs to perform well enough to prevent this from becoming a conversation.
Which week does Najee Harris take over as RB1? — Anonymous
It will be fascinating to see how this running back room shakes out. I’m confident Cam Skattebo will open the season as the No. 1 back. Harris could be anywhere from the No. 2 to inactive if the Giants don’t deem him fully ready to contribute. If it’s not by the opener, my sense is it won’t be long until he’s RB2. From there, workload distribution will depend on the performances of Harris and Skattebo. It wouldn’t surprise me if Harris becomes the lead back at some point this season.
It seems like Darius Slayton ended up in the doghouse. Is it because of his history of drops or did he lose a step coming off surgery? If it was the drops, could a player like Theo Johnson be in danger of falling into the doghouse, too? — Daniel A.
Slayton’s history of drops certainly hasn’t helped, and the double sports hernia surgery he had in the spring slowed him down. But he also just didn’t have a productive summer. He’s not new to the doghouse and has managed to claw out in the past, so it wouldn’t shock me if he does so again.
Johnson has the benefit of upside overshadowing some of his flaws. But continued drops will be a fast way to lose the faith of a new coaching staff. As it stands, Johnson is already in a complementary role to Likely.
Will John Michael Schmitz be the starting center by the 10th game? — Ed R.
Yes. The time to upgrade the starting center position was in March or April. It’s tough to upgrade a starter at this point in the calendar. The Giants like the upside of backup center Bryan Hudson, but he has essentially no game experience. It’s hard to imagine Schmitz playing so poorly that he gets benched midseason for Hudson.
Harbaugh has raved repeatedly about his cornerbacks. All I see is four question marks. Is it likely that a new system and an upgraded coaching staff can take these guys to the level Harbaugh expects? — Brian G.
Giants brass has insisted at every turn that it believes this is a quality group of cornerbacks. I can see the best case based on the pedigree: first-round picks Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome, second-round rookie Colton Hood and big-money veteran Paulson Adebo. But I’m skeptical. The faith in the corners is reminiscent of former general manager Dave Gettleman vowing the team had “more confidence in our offensive line than you guys do” before the group was a woeful disappointment in the 2021 season.
With Darius Alexander’s poor preseason, do you think the Giants should be confident that they have sufficient depth on the interior defensive line? — Nico U.
Nico’s question included a concern about pass rush at defensive tackle, but that shouldn’t be a major issue. The Giants will use Chauncey Golston, Kayvon Thibodeaux and Abdul Carter inside on passing downs to boost the pass rush. The much bigger concern is the run…

title: Eagles mailbag: Optimism and pessimism for 2026, Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers projections The Eagles’ roster, potential trades, rookie expectations and Jalen Hurts’ future headline this week’s mailbag. Zach Berman 3
summary:
Philadelphia Eagles rookie tight end Eli Stowers, left, enters the 2026 season behind Dallas Goedert with modest expectations for his offensive role. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
The mailbag is always fun to open. It shows what’s on readers’ minds and confirms that consensus is hard to find. Consider this: One question suggests the Eagles have declined since last year; another wonders why the Eagles don’t get enough respect. There were questions about the roster, the rookies and the future. Let’s
full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles rookie tight end Eli Stowers, left, enters the 2026 season behind Dallas Goedert with modest expectations for his offensive role. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
The mailbag is always fun to open. It shows what’s on readers’ minds and confirms that consensus is hard to find. Consider this: One question suggests the Eagles have declined since last year; another wonders why the Eagles don’t get enough respect. There were questions about the roster, the rookies and the future. Let’s get right to them…
Note: The questions were lightly edited for clarity.
I cannot get over how much less talented this roster seems than it was at the same time last year. What’s more, they’ve clearly sacrificed the development of young players for fringe-vested veterans at the edge of the roster.
Three-part question: At what positions are they more talented this year than last year? Who are the truly ascendant players on this roster who can “add talent” simply through their improvement over their performance last year? Can you point to a time in your years on the beat where they have returned a team that has improved so little (at least on paper) from the previous year’s team? — Lex S.
I disagree that this roster is less talented than it was at the start of last season. They’ve downgraded at wide receiver, but I think they’re more talented (and one year more experienced) on defense, and they’re healthier across the board. But let’s tackle your questions one by one.
1. Among the outside additions, I’d point to cornerback and edge rusher as two positions that stand out. Riq Woolen was a major upgrade. Jonathan Greenard was one of the biggest acquisitions by any team this offseason. If you’re comparing it to this time last year before Jaelan Phillips was in the building, it’s a definite upgrade. And then there are internal upgrades, which get to your next question…
2. Most of the defense would fit this category: Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Jihaad Campbell, Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean, Drew Mukuba are all players who are still ascending. Many of them played at a high level last year, but there’s another gear. And a good chunk of the offense underperformed last year relative to expectations. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks could improve based on bigger roles. The offensive line could improve based on better health. Jalen Hurts could improve based on a different scheme. It’s reasonable to expect internal improvements — that’s not even an optimistic view; it seems realistic.
3. The years that stand out to me are 2021, 2018, 2023, and 2025. In 2021, the Eagles were clearly resetting the roster. They were not actively seeking major veteran additions. The draft was helpful, though. In 2023, the Eagles experienced a clear exodus of talent following the Super Bowl appearance. They had a solid offseason between the draft and trades, but they weren’t aggressive in the veteran market. Most of the money went to re-signing players. And they lost talent after Super Bowl victories in 2018 and 2025.
I think you’re discounting the significance of acquiring Greenard and Woolen. I’m with you on the lack of personnel upgrades on offense, but I have a harder time suggesting they didn’t improve. They just made a strength (the defense) even stronger.
Hey ZB, please help me make sense of why there’s a general consensus among analysts that the Eagles have the potential to not be good this year. We had an awful offense last year and still won the division on the back of our defense. Our defense may be even better this year, and I find it hard to believe our offense will be worse despite the time needed to adapt to the scheme changes. Why the Eagles hate out there?? — Josh C.
This is the other side of the coin. If Lex seems pessimistic about the Eagles, Josh is pushing back against any skepticism. I don’t think there’s that general consensus. The odds back up the favorable view of the team. And most projections have the Eagles winning the NFC East. I don’t think Eagles fans can play the “nobody believes in us” card, so I’ll push back on the premise.
I picked the Eagles to go 11-6. But I’d be lying if I said there’s no reason for concern. You said it’s hard to believe the Eagles will be worse on offense. I’m not certain about that. They’re undergoing a major scheme adjustment, and they traded one of the NFL’s best receivers. You can call it addition by subtraction; I don’t see it that way. It’s subtraction when you lose that type of talent. I’m bullish on DeVonta Smith this season, but a lot is riding on Makai Lemon’s development and Dontayvion Wicks emerging into a starting-caliber receiver. Jalen Hurts has experience in new schemes, but he needs to improve a passing offense that lost a star. It’s a big year for him, as has been discussed.
Ultimately, the offense’s success will come down to the running game. The offensive line must stay healthy-ish, and a few key players have recent injury histories. If the line stays healthy and the running game is back — something I think is a reasonable expectation — then the passing game will improve because the run and pass work off each other. It could look closer to 2024. But I think the skepticism about the team is that an offense that ranked in the bottom half of the league last season enters the season with questions, and that skepticism is fair.
Other than Markel Bell being a nice story, how does the depth look on our offensive line after cutting Myles Hinton and Cameron Williams? We feel receiver-heavy and QB-heavy, and feel like we lost depth because we decided to keep an extra QB, maybe even two extras and Elijah Moore feels like a stretch for playing time. — Blake K.
Williams and Hinton were not players who would have been expected to contribute this year. Instead, they prioritized an extra receiver who can contribute this year and the potential trade value of carrying another quarterback.
On the offensive line, I feel better about the depth than I did entering training camp. So does Howie Roseman. The interior offensive line depth was a major question. Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin both had strong summers. Neither carries much experience, but if there’s an injury on the interior, you feel more confident about them after seeing them in camp and the preseason.
At tackle, the Eagles have Bell and Fred Johnson. Bell showed promise during training camp and could be the swing tackle. Johnson was less consistent, but he has starting experience.
The reality is there’s always a dropoff when you lose high-end talent. The Eagles have high-end talent on the line. If they miss a starter or two for a week or two, they can manage. If they sustain multiple long-term injuries, I’d be more concerned. Then again, not many teams can survive multiple long-term injuries on the offensive line.
With many positions like tight end and offensive line, the Eagles always drafted their next generation as top picks to learn while playing with the starters they would replace. Are you surprised with how they are gambling on mid-round picks for O-line and have left TE empty for next year?  — Jonathan S.
It’s a fair question at offensive line. We’ll see how Markel Bell develops this year. The Eagles went four drafts without taking an offensive lineman in the first or second round. That has never happened before under Roseman. I can write that I expect them to hit offensive line hard in the next year or two, but I’ve said that during the past few years. They can’t control the board.
At tight end, it’s a different story. They drafted Eli Stowers for the exact reason you mentioned. They won’t be empty next year if Stowers develops as they hope. That’s the nuance to the Stowers questions this summer. The pick was made with 2027 and beyond in mind.
Who is the most likely player that the Eagles could acquire by trade, and what would it cost in terms of draft capital or a player-for-player deal? — Ben H.
The profile of player I think…

title: 49ers' Keion White opens up about his recovery from a gunshot wound White played in nine games for the 49ers last season after being traded by the New England Patriots. Vic Tafur 1
summary:
White played in nine games for the 49ers last season after being traded by the New England Patriots. Norm Hall / Getty Images
Keion White can smile at it now. The 49ers defensive end had a grueling offseason coming back from a gunshot wound to his right ankle, suffered during an altercation in the early-morning hours the Monday after Super Bowl 60.

full_text:
White played in nine games for the 49ers last season after being traded by the New England Patriots. Norm Hall / Getty Images
Keion White can smile at it now. The 49ers defensive end had a grueling offseason coming back from a gunshot wound to his right ankle, suffered during an altercation in the early-morning hours the Monday after Super Bowl 60.
“It’s different because it’s trauma instead of just, like, breaking an ankle with a sports-related injury,” White said Tuesday, talking about the injury publicly for the first time since it happened. “When you hurt yourself in football, there’s a protocol for damn near everything. Football players don’t just get shot every day.
“… I mean, I guess they do on this team,” White added in a moment of attempted levity, referencing an incident in which Niners receiver Ricky Pearsall was shot during an attempted robbery in August 2024. Pearsall made his NFL debut two months later.
“But, yeah, it’s not … it’s not a normal thing, getting shot,” White said.
In addition to the gunshot wound, White, 27, also spent part of this summer recovering from an abductor injury that caused him to miss a week of training camp. The 49ers will be counting on him in the season opener against the Rams next week in Australia, because defensive end Mykel Williams (knee) is out, Nick Bosa (knee) likely will be on a snap count, and Sam Okuayinonu (foot) and rookie Romello Height (ankle) are also both dealing with injuries.
The season opener is upon us, and it seems like more than seven months ago that White was wounded at 4 a.m., in a San Francisco nightclub following the nearby Super Bowl. The incident allegedly started when rapper Lil Baby and his group tried to get into a private event that White was hosting, according to a police spokesperson.
“It was a gunshot to the foot,” White said. “I broke my talus bone, so I had to have surgery — two screws in there. But, yeah, brush it off. (I) literally was making jokes as I was going to the hospital.”
White said he didn’t fear for his life, and he reportedly declined to identify his shooter. No suspect had been named.
“The funny part is, I was actually the one calming everybody else down,” he said. “I don’t really take a lot of things seriously. I didn’t even know I got shot until like five minutes after, as I was walking around.”
He still has those two screws in his ankle.
“So, I got screws in each ankle now, so I’m symmetrical” joked White, who suffered a prior ankle injury ahead of the 2021 college football season.
But he’s not caring any emotional baggage from the shooting.
“Mentally, I was cool,” White said. “Like, I wasn’t really mentally traumatized or anything like that. Unfortunately, I’ve been in a situation, growing up and everything, where they had a shooting before — this was just unfortunately my time. It wasn’t traumatic at all, really.”
The recovery, though, was taxing. White has been working with Lily Abdelmalek, who’s been his personal trainer since he was coming out of Georgia Tech and getting ready for the NFL scouting combine in 2023.
“He spent a lot of time in physical therapy this year before we actually started the training regimen,” said Abdelmalek in a phone interview. “There was more one-on-one training, rather than group offseason training — making sure that he was getting in shape and getting the same type of power that he once had before the gunshot.”
“I think we got him to where he needed to be.”
The 6-foot-5, 285-pound White is moving well, and the 49ers remain happy they traded a sixth-round pick to the Patriots for him last season.
White, a second-round pick in 2023, had six sacks in his first two seasons with the Patriots but largely felt misused in that scheme — and the 49ers agreed. They like moving him inside on passing downs, when he is not helping set the edge on the outside.
White is also taking on a leadership role for the younger players, both with the 49ers and among those who worked out with him during his offseason program, where Abedelmalek and her team train roughly 40 NFL players.
“He was already the type of person that, when faced with any type of injury or setback, he will always be on top of it,” Abdelmalek said. “And he just has a natural talent, being as explosive as he is and with the kind of power that he has. And now, he’s been able to mentor younger guys coming in.”
For his part, White is excited about Height and another rookie defensive tackle, Gracen Halton. He’s eager for the 49ers to kick off the regular season, too.
And though the shooting is out of mind — ironically, White might be the healthiest defensive end on the team — the ankle still bears some daily upkeep.
“To be honest, it’s still an ongoing thing,” White said. “Still recovering, taking it a day at a time. But I feel pretty good right now. It was like a touch-and-go situation right up to the beginning of training camp, for real.”

full_text:
Jayden Daniels looks to bounce back after injuries and inconsistencies limited his second pro campaign. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
After going 12-5 and reaching the NFC Championship Game in 2024, the Washington Commanders fell to 5-12 last season and missed the playoffs. Injuries played a substantial role in the reversal, with quarterback Jayden Daniels and WR1 Terry McLaurin missing significant time. A defense with some obvious limitations in 2024 then dropped to last in the league in yards allowed.
As expected, the Commanders spent much of the offseason trying to recapture what worked two years ago.
Head coach Dan Quinn and general manager Adam Peters return for their third season together in Washington, but both coordinator positions have changed hands. David Blough was promoted from assistant quarterbacks coach to run the offense, while Daronte Jones was hired as the new defensive coordinator. Blough is a first-time play caller, but he’s worked closely with Daniels since his rookie season.
Everything the Commanders want to do offensively depends on Daniels being healthy, and they gave him more options at the skill positions this offseason. They added veteran receiver Stefon Diggs, as well as tight end Chig Okonkwo and running back Rachaad White.
The defense underwent an aggressive overhaul, bringing in edge rushers Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson, linebacker Leo Chenal, defensive lineman Charles Omenihu, cornerback Amik Robertson and safety Nick Cross. They also used the No. 7 overall pick on Ohio State linebacker Sonny Styles.
The 2026 schedule puts Washington in almost every major NFL television window. The Commanders have four primetime games on the docket, plus a Week 4 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts in London. Weeks 16, 17 and 18 remain TBD, leaving open the possibility of additional national games late in the season.
Before getting into the guide for all 17 games, make sure you’re following the Commanders and senior writer Nicki Jhabvala on The Athletic for year-round coverage.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI

title: Michael Wilson Got His Payday — But He Wants a Cardinals Turnaround Even More
full_text:
ARIZONA — Today felt like a massive win for the Arizona Cardinals, their fans, and Michael Wilson all in one swoop.
The ink is still drying on Wilson's contract extension with the organization, to the tune of a three-year deal worth $25 million annually. Reports indicate the contract can be worth up to $78 million total with incentives.
Wilson got paid, leaping the likes of Christian Watson and Michael Pittman Jr. this offseason after both signed their respective deals. The Cardinals keep what they hope to be a core piece of their team for the foreseeable future, and fans finally see a drafted and developed talent under general manager Monti Ossenfort sign an extension.
The Cardinals haven't won the division in over a decade. They also haven't been in a playoff game since 2021. There's been glimpses of hope they could turn things around, but nothing more than a flash in the pan.
That could potentially change under new head coach Mike LaFleur, who has spoke so glowingly of Wilson and what he could potentially be in the offense.
Wilson could have opted to chase more money or find a new team after this season. However, he stuck around — and he wants to be part of the reason the Cardinals turn things around.
"I love the organization. I love living in the state of Arizona. I love the people in Arizona, and I think when you can be a centerpiece and flip something, that's way more gratifying and rewarding," Wilson said when asked why he re-signed with the Cardinals.
"Going through the dark days, the tough times, when you've lost bad games, when there's more Niner fans than Arizona fans. Like, how cool would that be this season when the stadium's packed and we're in a race for the playoffs or a playoff team and we're in the playoffs? Being a centerpiece of changing, like turning the tides. I think that sense of loyalty — that just screams the type of player and person that I want to be.
"I want to be a centerpiece to a franchise and be a guy that was a cornerstone piece that helped flip it. What better place to do it in Arizona? I keep saying it, but I got so much love for Arizona. I genuinely do, and not even tied to the franchise — I can see myself living here for the rest of my life. So I want to bring good vibes, wins to the fan base and to the organization.
"I definitely feel a sense of debt, and I'm gonna work my hardest every single day to show why I deserve that deal."

title: Michael Wilson Admits He Wasn't Sure Cardinals Contract Would Get Done
full_text:
ARIZONA — Even Michael Wilson was swept up in contract rumors before putting pen to paper .
24 hours ago, the Arizona Cardinals' receiver didn't know if an extension was going to be reached before the start of the regular season. With today being the final day of practice before the team parts for the weekend, there was an unofficial but hopeful deadline for Wilson and the Cardinals to strike a deal.
Wilson and Arizona indeed found a middle ground, reaching an agreement on a three-year, $75 million deal that can be worth up to $78 million — $47 million was guaranteed.
However, Wilson himself admitted to reporters he wasn't so sure something would get done.
"Talks have been going on since early offseason, and so I definitely wanted to get the deal done prior to Week 1, just for obvious reasons. And one, I wanted to know that I had security being in Arizona, but I think everyone saw the report yesterday," Wilson said near the beginning of his press conference.
The report came from ESPN's Dan Graziano, who suggested the Cardinals and Wilson were so far off that numerous sources told him Wilson was likely to hit free agency.
Yet the tide turned quickly to ensure Wilson wouldn't hit the open market next offseason.
"Things, conversations happened, tides turned, and the deal happened to get done. I couldn't even sleep last night, I was just so excited. I'm just so excited it got done."
Wilson also said contract talks were long and the two sides sometimes went weeks without communication.
"They were long. I'm not going to say I was nervous about it not getting done, but there were times where both sides, we didn't speak for a couple weeks and kind of reevaluating things," Wilson added.
"But I try to stay out of it as much as possible and let my agent handle it because — I said this early in offseason — like I didn't want to let a contract dictate how I played, performed, and the way that I showed up for my coaches and teammates throughout the offseason.
"So I tried my best to stay out of it and not bring it onto the field, not bring it into the locker room, and let Monti [Ossenfort] and his team handle it, my team handle it."
The Cardinals and Wilson both ultimately emerge as winners — Arizona retains arguably their top receiver at the moment while Wilson gets an annual contract value of $25 million per season.
And sometimes, that winning shot comes at the buzzer.

title: Cardinals Extend Michael Wilson — 4 More Players Who Could Be Next
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals have now completed their second official extension and third re-worked contract of the 2026 offseason.
Wide receiver Michael Wilson's new $78 million contract extension becomes the latest of deals from general manager Monti Ossenfort ahead of the regular season, falling in line after starting center Hjalte Froholdt and quarterback Jacoby Brissett put pen to paper as well.
The Cardinals now have one of their top playmakers under contract for the foreseeable future — who's next?
4 extension candidates in the desert:
Johnson, a first-round pick in Wilson's draft class, also became extension eligible this past offseason. With him being Ossenfort's first draft pick, there's some sentimental value here.
However, Johnson's earned a payday. Despite finishing the last two seasons on injured reserve, he's played at near Pro Bowl levels after making the switch from right tackle. Johnson is by no means an All-Pro talent (yet), though when you find quality players like Johnson, you keep them around.
Especially at one of football's most important positions, and protecting whoever is the future face of the franchise.
Wilson is undoubtedly the heartbeat of Arizona's front seven, and if you need any evidence of that, just look at last season.
His departure due to a season-ending rib injury saw the Cardinals' defense take a nose dive, and Arizona is excited to have one of their top leaders back in the mix.
Yet he's not only valuable in the locker room — his athleticism to drop into coverage and play as a pass defender with versatility to plug the run and rush the passer makes him a valuable asset in this defense.
Linebacker is sometimes a volatile position, though Wilson is 28 and has plenty to offer if for nothing else than a short-term extension before he hits free agency this summer.
Williams was graded as one of Pro Football Focus' best cornerbacks entering last season before suffering a string of injuries that sidelined him for seven games, the latest being a season-ending Achilles injury that put his status for 2026's season opener in doubt.
However, Williams has made a full recovery and is off the injured list. Now, it's up to Williams to bounce back and reach the previous levels he once displayed as one of the league's top slot cornerbacks with versatility to play on the boundary or some safety, too.
If he can stay healthy this season, it feels like a no-brainer.
It feels like Dante Stills can never get enough love.
The Cardinals' defensive lineman is a quiet but consistent contributor in Arizona's defense. No, he's not a first-round pick like Darius Robinson or Walter Nolen III is. He also doesn't have fan popularity like local product Roy Lopez, either.
However, what Stills does is put his head down at a high level and produces when called upon. Losing him wouldn't be the end of the world, but he does provide stable play in the trenches while also raising the Cardinals' floor as well.

title: Michael Wilson's $78M Cardinals Extension: What We Really Think
full_text:
ARIZONA — The dust is beginning to settle on Michael Wilson's contract extension with the Arizona Cardinals.
It's a good one, for both sides.
Wilson officially has inked a three-year contract reportedly worth up to $78 million with an annual average of $25 million per season. Wilson was entering the final year of his rookie contract, and the Cardinals wanted to strike a deal before the season.
That goal was ultimately achieved, and we've got some thoughts:
Spotrac had the Cardinals' receiver at $18 million per season in terms of annual market value for a new contract. Wilson comes in at $25 million per season, outpacing recently extended receivers in Christian Watson and Michael Pittman Jr.
Wilson's career figures were similar to Watson, so the annual average of $25 million compared to Watson's $23 million isn't that crazy of a bump. The $47 million guaranteed isn't an eye-opening number, either.
Still, some were doubting Wilson's ability to get paid based on Trey McBride and Marvin Harrison Jr.'s presence in the desert. Wilson answered with a massive win at the negotiation table.
Drafting and developing is imperative to building a solid foundation for organizational success. The Cardinals just saw Monti Ossenfort's first draft class become eligible to be extended this offseason with Wilson and Paris Johnson Jr. leading the way.
Ossenfort has previously handled big contract talks with players such as Budda Baker and McBride, though he's yet to be tasked with inking guys he personally drafted since taking over in 2023.
Handling business and securing a talented player in-house for the foreseeable future was massive not only for the fan base, but also for Arizona's locker room as well. It's a boost for the players not only in terms of morale for their teammate, but also knowing the front office will reward them as well.
The Cardinals' top playmakers are under contract for the next two seasons, at minimum.
McBride's on his record-setting extension. Wilson is now paid. Fresh draft pick Jeremiyah Love is now on the books for one of the league's top running back contracts, too.
Harrison is set to play in his third season in the league with some fairly inconsistent play under his belt. The talent is obvious — the production hasn't matched. After this year, the Cardinals have a massive decision coming on his fifth-year option.
If picked up, he'll be under contract through 2028. If declined, he'll be a free agent after his fourth season (2027).
Harrison is also eligible for a contract extension next offseason, which places the former No. 4 overall pick in a precarious position.
Between McBride, Wilson and Love, that's now $97 million combined in average annual salary. Will Arizona want to commit even more substantial money in the future to Harrison?
That question can surely be answered and perhaps even justified with a big 2026 campaign from Harrison. However, Arizona will also need to lock down their franchise tackle in Johnson along with improving other potential spots such as edge rusher and perhaps even quarterback next offseason.
If Harrison matches Wilson's $25 million annual mark, that make the Cardinals one of four NFL teams to have multiple wideouts earning that dollar amount or higher, joining the Cincinnati Bengals, Detroit Lions and Dallas Cowboys.
Now, there's less salary cap wiggle room for Harrison in the future. He needs to perform this season.

title: Cardinals Legend Gets Honest on Michael Wilson's Contract Dilemma
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and wide receiver Michael Wilson has the entire NFL world buzzing.
Conflicting reports have emerged on Wilson's contract negotiations with the Cardinals ahead of the 2026 season. Some have suggested the Cardinals and Wilson aren't close while others believe a deal could come to fruition soon.
It's an incredibly complex situation that requires nuance and understanding from both sides.
A franchise legend in Adrian Wilson recently took to social media to shed some light on Arizona's contract battle with their big wideout:
I just want to add my two little cents in on the whole Michael Wilson and @AZCardinals trying to get an extension done. At the end of the day yes there is a right number for both parties. When I say this I’m saying it with my whole chest.
Through a string of posts on X, Wilson gave his two cents on what's going on:
"It sucks that ownership continually gets blamed for something not working. Look agents have a huge deal in this and let’s be honest the market is through the roof for wide receivers. Is Michael Wilson a #1 probably not. He’s a good solid steady player," he said.
"High value #2 that can compliment your #1 and for the  @AZCardinals that’s Trey McBride right now not Marvin Harrison. The thought is that Marvin will present himself to be the guy and I’m rooting for him because the team needs his production.
"You can’t pay Michael Wilson 20+ plus million while having thoughts about Marvin Harrison being your true #1 on the O/S. Just doesn’t make you feel good as a front office. No offense to Michael Wilson it’s just true.
"It’s probably best they wait till after the season to see how it plays out.
"Reminds me of Anquan Boldin and Larry Fitzgerald having contract conversations and at the end of the day Anquan was the freaking dude but Fitz had already resigned to a damn near fully guaranteed contract.
"So what was the team to do if it couldn’t get to the number that Q wanted. It’s just so hard to juggle those numbers at one position. Same thing happened with Antrel Rolle and myself. He ended up going to the Giants because the numbers just didn’t align.
"Don’t talk to me about Tee Higgins and Jamar Chase either because the defense suffered for having multiple high number players at one position. At the end of the day it has to be logical balance.
"Also people are trying to keep their jobs as well so that plays a role too. Anyway, wasn’t trying to offend but I do have some experience in this area. Just my thoughts though."

title: Deep Dive: Why Michael Wilson and the Cardinals Are Playing a Dangerous Game
full_text:
*UPDATE: Michael Wilson has signed an extension! You can read more about that here .
Contract talks between the Arizona Cardinals and receiver Michael Wilson have reportedly stalled ahead of the 2026 season, per ESPN. All indications point to Wilson becoming one of the biggest free agents next offseason.
Over the course of the summer, both Wilson and the Cardinals insisted a deal is desired. Wilson stated he wasn't going to let the contract be a distraction while general manager Monti Ossenfort was clear in wanting to keep Wilson around long-term.
While that might be true, player and organization have their personal interests in mind first — and both sides appear to be willing to gamble this season.
Ossenfort's entering his fourth season running the Cardinals since taking over ahead of the 2023 season.
Ossenfort's extended big names in previous seasons, with all of Budda Baker, James Conner and most recently Trey McBride putting pen to paper on new deals. Former first-round pick Zaven Collins can also be looped here as well while Arizona just recently extended starting center Hjalte Froholdt.
The Cardinals, obviously, haven't been shy on keeping around their biggest names. And if you want to count the reworked deal for Jacoby Brissett this summer too, feel free.
Yet for a team that's intent on drafting and developing, the time to pay their homegrown players is finally here after three full seasons under Ossenfort's watch.
Oftentimes the line between simple negotiating tactics and lowballing can be blurred in these instances. To accuse the Cardinals of doing the latter would be a bit harsh, though McBride's comments on a recent podcast may have peeled the curtain back on how Ossenfort and co. approach business.
"The first offer, it was actually way lower, it was like $12 million. The Cardinals are a tough deal," said McBride when reflecting on negotiations.
"I was like, 'yeah, it might not be the Cardinals, maybe I go somewhere else. Maybe I play my last year and kind of explore my options, and then they finally wanted to get it done."
As fate would have it, the Cardinals made McBride the highest-paid tight end in NFL history — but not without a bit of sparring first.
Every negotiation is different based off player and circumstance. You can't really correlate McBride and Wilson's negotiations (like throwing an apple in the orange bin), though perhaps that sets the table for understanding Arizona's side of the table.
Wilson suffered an injury-riddled college career at Stanford before having a strong week at the Senior Bowl, which shot his stock up and eventually landed in the desert as a third-round pick. His size as a 6-2 receiver with contested catch ability made him an attractive addition to any receiver room.
Health has been on Wilson's side for his three-year NFL stint, missing just four games in that time. Unfortunately, opportunity has not.
Wilson's rookie season was spent behind Marquise Brown and Rondale Moore. In 2024 he saw an increase in targets from 58 to 71, though a breakout season from McBride and fresh No. 4 overall pick Marvin Harrison Jr.'s presence stalled any progress.
That appeared to again be a trend through the first five games of 2025, where Wilson caught just eight passes for 52 yards and one score.
However, a mix of a change at quarterback with Brissett under center , a revamped offensive approach to throw the ball more and injuries to Harrison cleared the way for Wilson to break out in 2025, ultimately finishing strong with 78 receptions for 1,006 yards and seven touchdowns.
Wilson had continually made plays when called upon in previous years. When opportunity knocked last season, he answered big time. And now, Wilson approaches 2026 as arguably Arizona's top receiver. He's looking to be paid like one.
That late surge made him millions in the future. It also makes the Cardinals hesitate.
We've established the track records for both sides, and unless a dramatic change of events happens, it doesn't look like an extension gets done soon.
Ossenfort didn't rule out any extensions happening during the middle of the season, though it does feel like the Cardinals and Wilson each might want to let events play out.
For Wilson, he's been a reliable staple in the Cardinals' WR room since walking through the door. He's arguing that 2025 was the first opportunity he had to be a primary weapon, and even with McBride having a historic season, Wilson still managed to put up close to 1,000 yards in 12 games.
Arizona isn't buying it. We don't know exactly what Wilson is asking for, but as a rule of negotiations you either start high/low and meet in the middle. Perhaps Wilson is asking for eye-opening money, perhaps he isn't — the Cardinals however don't want to call in the BRINKS truck simply based off of 12 games in three seasons.
Wilson's agent, Andrew Kessler of Athletes First, has experience getting big names top dollar. He's been at the helm or involved in negotiations representing Jordan Love, Michael Thomas, Drake London and Michael Pittman Jr. in recent years among others.
He knows how to get receivers paid, and for what it's worth, he does represent new Cardinals RB Tyler Allgeier and recently QB Clayton Tune, so there's somewhat of a relationship already built with Arizona in these negotiations.
The wide receiver position has seen substantial growth over the years, and within the next few years that's expected to boom even more with NFL TV rights set to be renegotiated — which should only juice the salary cap even more.
Spotrac's data projects Wilson's market value at $18.3 million per season on a new contract.
At this moment, Jaxon Smith-Njigba paces all NFL receivers at $42.1 million per season. Only Ja'Marr Chase is with him in the $40M AAV while eleven more wideouts eclipse $30 million annually and 14 more at $20 million or higher.
Wilson is very unlikely to hit $30 million per season — in fact that would be a massive win that would require cases of champagne for Wilson and his camp.
However, his numbers are comparable to two freshly extended receivers in Christian Watson and Pittman, perhaps providing a solid ceiling and floor of what to expect. Wilson's career numbers mirror Watson while last year's production is closer to Pittman's.
Christian Watson Extension : 4 YR, $92 MILLION TOTAL, $23 MILLION AAV Michael Pittman Jr. Extension: 2 YR, $35 MILLION TOTAL, $17.5 MILLION AAV
Wilson, if inked this year at 26 years old, would be younger than Watson (28) and Pittman (27) at signing, though he's got less experience than Watson (entering his fifth year in 2026) and Pittman (seventh).
Much has been made about the Cardinals' future spending power, and maybe rightfully so. Arizona, using OverTheCap's projections for 2027, has the most amount of space next offseason for the entire league.
In terms of "effective" cap that already factors in money needed to sign the draft class, the Cardinals are sitting at a projected $107.9 M at this moment in time.
Those figures can and will change, though the bottom line remains: that's some serious spending power.
However, Wilson isn't the only one up for an extension. The likes of Garrett Williams, Paris Johnson Jr. Dante Stills and Mack Wilson among others are set to be free agents. Additionally, players such as Marvin Harrison Jr. will become extension eligible after completing their third season.
All of those players and potential deals play a factor into Arizona's cap health. That's on top of potentially looking to solve massive puzzles at tackle, edge rusher and perhaps even quarterback next offseason as well.
There's room for numerous moves, but the Cardinals have to be careful and diligent on how they allocate those resources. Oftentimes teams spend big in free agency and fail to do anything when football goes from spreadsheets to grass.
That's not to say that would be the case if/when Wilson signs, though general managers have a puzzle they must carefully construct each offseason.

title: Cardinals Adding Former Steelers DB
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are adding former Pittsburgh Steelers and Carolina Panthers cornerback D’Shawn Jamison to their practice squad, according to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz.
Jamison worked out for the team today before signing his contract, according to the NFL's transaction wire.
The Cardinals only kept five cornerbacks on their active roster. Starting cornerback Will Johnson suffered what head coach Mike LaFleur described as a "lower body injury" to reporters with no clarity on when he's expected back on the field.
Jamison, listed at 5-10 and 185 lbs, just turned 27 this past June and initially entered the league as an undrafted free agent in 2023 after playing five years of college football at Texas.
Jamison signed with the San Francisco 49ers that summer before being waived ahead of final roster cuts. He was claimed by Carolina the next day and appeared in 15 games for the Panthers with one start.
He mostly featured on special teams, playing 39% of snaps.
Ahead of 2024 roster cuts, he was waived and eventually picked up by the Steelers. He remained on their practice squad through the last two years and appeared in three games for Pittsburgh last season – all of his snaps came on special teams.
Jamison was waived by the Steelers this past weekend as part of final roster cuts.
Now, he arrives to the Cardinals with a familiar face in senior defensive assistant Teryl Austin, who spent recent years as the Steelers' defensive coordinator. The familiarity and relationship most likely played a role in helping Jamison land in the desert.
The Cardinals have just over ten days until their regular season opener against the Los Angeles Chargers. They didn't claim anybody on waivers after establishing their initial 53-man roster.

title: Cardinals' QB Problem Is Nowhere Near as Bad as You Think
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals quarterback situation is being called one of the worst in the NFL.
It's tough to overlook the uphill battle Arizona faces this season. After firing head coach Jonathan Gannon and releasing former No. 1 overall pick Kyler Murray, the Cardinals — stuck in the league's toughest division — aren't projected to do much in 2026.
Jacoby Brissett , back in the saddle after his holdout, leads the way with veteran backup Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck behind. Brissett and Minshew are on one-year deals while the third-round pick in Beck was injured for most of preseason with playing time unknown for the regular season.
It's not the prettiest, surely. The Athletic made that known when ranking the team's quarterback situation the third-worst in the league only behind the New York Jets and Cleveland Browns.
"If you’re in a situation where you not only have Brissett holding out over a contract dispute but, as a team, you decide to give in to his demands, things are not going well. In fairness to Arizona, it didn’t appear the Cardinals had any intention of fielding high-level quarterback play this season," wrote Saad Yousuf.
LaFleur's offense has been nothing short of exciting this offseason, providing a glimpse of hope and perhaps a massive breath of fresh air from prior play-caller Drew Petzing. LaFleur's unit looks strong regardless of who is operating the offense under center, and players' comments on the new system indeed matches the eye test.
Still, the conversation seems to shift around Brissett — who isn't as polarizing as Murray once was here in the desert, though fans are often split. There seems to be a rush to put Beck into action sooner as opposed to later thanks to a mix of public opinion on Brissett and purely wanting to evaluate Beck ahead of a potentially loaded 2027 draft class.
However, Brissett is more suitable than people give him credit for.
While the overall outlook of the Cardinals' quarterback picture is murky for the future, Brissett projects as a fine quarterback to steady the ship in 2026.
The problem with Brissett is his ceiling — he's not the type of quarterback to will a team to victory. He doesn't do anything at an extremely high level and won't keep coordinators up at night with any potential to scare defenses.
The good news? LaFleur's offense doesn't need hero ball. It needs a quarterback to simply make smart decisions and keep the offense humming on schedule.
Brissett's profile does fit just that. It's impossible to ignore the elephant in the room with Brissett's career highs in passing yards and touchdowns last season: Arizona was getting blown out, and the Cardinals consistently were throwing the ball in an attempt to keep pace.
Last season, nobody attempted more passes than the Cardinals.
With that acknowledged, it's obvious players such as Michael Wilson and Trey McBride loved having Brissett under center after both reached 1,000-yard seasons. Brissett's experience allows him to make reads quickly and mostly efficiently — his 1.6% interception percentage of throws sat just outside of the top ten for quarterbacks last season.
Brissett certainly was limited in his own respects last season. In fact, he was only supposed to be a backup for Murray — which is what his two-year contract reflected when signing ahead of 2025. If he starts every game this season, it will be just the first time since 2017 where he started and ended the season in that seat.
Unlikely? Sure, but probably not for the reasons you think.
For as much as Brissett fell short in potential and ceiling as a player, a significant lack of run game mixed with one of the league's worst defenses down the stretch of last season snowballed into something no quarterback in the league could overcome.
We also have to acknowledge some of the Brissett slander online was a result of Murray effectively being "soft benched" by the Cardinals after his injury.
A new and improved play-caller and revamped rushing attack should make for a smoother operation. However, the NFL's toughest schedule and a mostly same returning unit from the Cardinals' defense will provide a similar challenge for Brissett.
We also have to acknowledge Beck's presence in the quarterback room. It's tough to think Arizona, who will face one of the biggest decisions in recent franchise history next offseason at quarterback, will make such a heavy judgement with only one preseason game of Beck's play.
Brissett is not a great enough quarterback to overcome many of the aforementioned challenges that lie ahead. In the same boat, he's also not an unprepared or incompetent quarterback like plenty outside of the facility paint him to be.

title: 5 NFL Matchup Nightmares Who Could Wreck Atlanta Falcons’ 2026 Season
full_text:
On paper, the Atlanta Falcons have one of the weakest NFL schedules for the 2026 season, but it sure doesn’t line up that way, especially early in the season.
Starting on the road at the Pittsburgh Steelers next Sunday, Sept. 13, Atlanta’s 17-game slate is the fourth easiest across the league’s 32 teams , according to ESPN. Based on last season’s win percentage, the Falcons’ opponents have a combined winning percentage of .465.
But don’t expect it to be a cakewalk in Atlanta. The team faces brutal stretches and many of the NFL’s brightest stars.
That means the Falcons’ hopes of reaching the NFL playoffs could very easily vanish if they don’t come to play under first-year head coach Kevin Stefanski .
Here are player matches who could hinder the Falcons’ turnaround efforts this fall.
Despite inconsistencies and a shaky start to his three-year NFL career, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young has become the Falcon beater . He holds a 4-1 record as a starter against the NFC South rival. Meanwhile, he’s 14-30 overall under center in Carolina.
Last season, he led a Carolina sweep over the Falcons, including an embarrassing 30-0 win in their first matchup. Young then followed that act with a record-breaking performance in November. He completed 31 of 45 pass attempts for a franchise record of 448 yards and tossed three touchdowns en route to winning the Division and leading the Panthers to the playoffs.
The Falcons and Panthers meet twice for divisional battles early in Week 2 and late in Week 18, which could ultimately have playoff implications in the logjammed NFC South.
Two-time MVP Lamar Jackson’s dual-threat ability creates a hurdle for the Falcons’ defense. Though the Falcons had a franchise-record 57 sacks in 2025 , they struggled to stop the run. And Jackson, the quarterback record holder for most career rushing yards, adds an extra runner on the field for the Falcons.
It will be quite an early-season test for Atlanta on Sunday Night Football in the second season with Jeff Ulbrich as defensive coordinator . A positive sign was that the Falcons didn’t struggle much with mobile quarterbacks last season, facing the likes of MVP Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen and former Arizona Cardinals signal-caller Kyler Murray, now the starter for the Minnesota Vikings.
But Jackson is on a different level as a scrambler.
A.J. Terrell will have a chance to continue to prove himself as a franchise cornerback for his hometown team, Atlanta. He’ll be paired up against Bengals star wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase in the NFL Madrid game.
It’ll add another chapter to the wide receiver-cornerback matchup. Many likely remember when Chase, as a member of the LSU Tigers, routinely beat Terrell, of Clemson, in the 2020 NCAA College Football Playoff National Championship game. Chase finished with nine receptions, 221 yards, and two touchdowns.
Terrell and Chase also briefly met in the 2022 NFL season, but the Falcons’ corner left the game early after a hamstring injury. Four years later, Terrell will hold a big responsibility of shadowing Chase and limiting his targets to force Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow to look elsewhere to throw.
Love him or hate him, three-time Super Bowl champion and MVP quarterback Patrick Mahomes finds a way to win. Many Falcons fans will call back to Atlanta’s controversial 22-17 Sunday Night Football loss in 2024 . The refs swallowed their flags as Kyle Pitts was mugged in the end zone.
The Falcons can exact retribution for that. But it won’t be an easy task. It’ll start up front. The Falcons’ pass rush must beleaguer Mahomes, fresh off a torn ACL and LCL. Atlanta will have to do so without its rising star pass rusher Jalon Walker, who’s out for the season with a torn ACL .
However, James Pearce Jr. will be back for his second game after his NFL suspension for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.
Detroit edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson can play both sides of the defensive line. But if he lines up on the left side, that could spell trouble for Atlanta. The Falcons don’t have the best situation at right tackle, the blindside for whoever starts at quarterback between lefties Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa .
Jawaan Taylor is the presumed starting right tackle, but he is the most penalized in the NFL . Another option is Michael Jerrell, but he’s a developmental piece. An All-Pro defensive end like Hutchinson would be licking his chops at his matchups. He comes off picking up 14.5 sacks for the Lions a season ago.
The Falcons enter the season on the road against the Aaron Rodgers-led Steelers next Sunday.
Kickoff in Pittsburgh is at 1 p.m. on FOX.

title: Atlanta Falcons Don't Name a QB among 3 First-Time Captains as New Era Begins
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have named their five team captains for the 2026 season; the franchise enters a new era under head coach Kevin Stefanski.
Running back Bijan Robinson, offensive lineman Chris Lindstrom, safety Jessie Bates III, inside linebacker Divine Deablo, and kicker Nick Folk were voted captains by their teammates. Robinson, Deablo, and Folk are first-time captains. Bates returns as a four-time captain, while Lindstrom earns the honor for the third time.
Bates III Deablo Folk Lindstrom Robinson Inside the huddle for the captains announcement 🔥 pic.twitter.com/j753PIptnx
The Falcons’ decision is notable because there is no quarterback among this year’s five captains. Atlanta is still waiting to make its decision on a starting quarterback for the regular season, making the leadership group even more important heading into Week 1.
The 2026 captains also represent a significant change from last season.
In 2025, the Falcons’ six captains were quarterback Michael Penix Jr., Lindstrom, Jake Matthews, Bates, Kaden Elliss and Bradley Pinion. Lindstrom and Bates are the only two players from that group to retain the honor this season.
That turnover comes as Atlanta moves from the Raheem Morris era into Stefanski’s first season as head coach.
Stefanski’s first coaching staff also represents a new direction for the organization, including new offensive coordinator Tommy Rees and offensive line coach Bill Callahan, while defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich and running backs coach Michael Pitre were retained.
In that transition, having respected players establish the team’s standard becomes especially important.
Captains aren’t simply ceremonial leaders. They can serve as a bridge between players and coaches, help establish accountability, communicate expectations inside the locker room, and provide leadership when adversity hits. They also represent the team during pregame ceremonies and other official responsibilities.
For Robinson, Deablo and Folk, their selections show that their teammates see them as more than contributors on the field.
Robinson is now one of the faces of the franchise, Deablo will provide another leadership voice on defense, and Folk brings veteran experience to special teams.
Meanwhile, Lindstrom and Bates provide continuity from previous seasons.
The Falcons are entering 2026 with a new coaching philosophy, a revamped football operation, and several unanswered questions. Their captains will be responsible for helping turn that transition into a unified locker room as they head into the regular season.
The Falcons will face the Steelers on the road in Pittsburgh on Sunday, Sept. 13 for the Week 1 opener of the 2026 season.

title: Falcons GM Ian Cunningham Sends Strong Message on Billy Bowman Jr.’s Recovery
full_text:
Atlanta Falcons defensive back Billy Bowman Jr.’s rookie season ended before he had the chance to truly establish himself in the NFL.
Now, nearly a year removed from a devastating Achilles injury, he's finally taking another major step toward getting back on the field.
General manager Ian Cunningham has been impressed with the work Bowman Jr. has put into his recovery.
“Yeah, really, really proud of Billy, man. It’s a testament to him, his work ethic, his resilience, the time in which he’s put into his body to fight to get back,” Cunningham said.
Bowman suffered that torn Achilles during a Friday walkthrough in November 2025 ahead of Atlanta’s Week 12 matchup against the New Orleans Saints. The injury required surgery and prematurely ended his rookie season after just six appearances and one start.
Despite the limited sample size, Bowman made an impact during his first season. He recorded 19 tackles, one interception and one pass breakup in six games, showing enough for the Falcons to remain invested in his development entering 2026.
Bowman began this year’s training camp on the active/PUP list while continuing his rehabilitation. Atlanta has now removed him from PUP, although Cunningham made it clear that doesn’t mean Bowman is immediately ready for game action.
“Now when that time will be, I can’t tell you. But we do feel comfortable enough to not keep him on PUP, so I think that should say something,” Cunningham said.
If he had remained on the PUP list to start the season, he would have had to miss at least the first four games of the season.
The Falcons are taking a cautious approach with Bowman as he works his way back from one of football’s most significant injuries.
“A lot of credit also goes to our return-to-play staff putting an outstanding plan together in order for him to come back and feel confident,” Cunningham said.
Bowman’s recovery also comes at an interesting time for Atlanta’s secondary.
The Falcons elected to carry a large group of defensive backs on their roster , creating significant competition for playing time and roles. That depth gives Atlanta the luxury of allowing Bowman to progress at his own pace rather than forcing him back before he’s ready.
Cunningham pointed to Bowman as an example of the type of resilience the Falcons are seeing throughout the entire roster.
“The beauty is we have a lot of players like that. What we’re seeing is we have a lot of players that are fighting to get back, that are resilient, that are willing to fight through some nicks. But in Billy’s case, he’s done a really good job,” Cunningham said.
For Bowman, the next objective isn’t necessarily getting back into the starting lineup immediately. It’s continuing to clear each stage of the rehabilitation process and eventually proving that he can return to the level of play he showed before the Achilles injury.
Bowman is finally moving closer to a return. And based on Cunningham’s comments, the Falcons believe the work he’s put in has positioned him well for a quick return to the lineup.
